*This report is adapted from Modern Retail’s sibling publication Digiday. You can read the* [full report on Digiday](https://digiday.com/media-buying/digiday-media-agency-report-2026-how-agencies-adapt-to-a-media-landscape-shaped-by-ai-and-creators/).

Media agencies are navigating an increasingly complex advertising landscape, as economic uncertainty, fragmented media consumption and rapid advances in technology continue to reshape how brands reach consumers.

AI search and creator marketing are adding another layer of change to the agency landscape, creating opportunities to expand services while raising new questions about costs, capabilities and the future of media planning.

Bearing this in mind, Modern Retail+ Research examined how agencies and their clients are adapting to these shifts, from media spending and channel investment to creator partnerships and the evolving role of AI.

To understand how agencies and their clients are working with creators and implementing AI, Modern Retail+ Research collected responses from 30 agency professionals in a survey fielded in third-quarter 2026. For additional industry insight, Modern Retail hosted a focus group of five senior media agency executives who oversee media investment and technology.

Agencies that participated in the focus group were:

- Go Fish Digital
- Horizon Media
- Novus
- Tinuiti
- UM

When Modern Retail asked agencies and brands how important creator marketing has become to their business over the last year, the overwhelming majority of respondents (75%) said that creator marketing has become at least a little or significantly more important in the past 12 months.

Focus group participants noticed an uptick in creator partnerships as well, including a shift in the type of work brands are asking creators to produce. “On the creator side, we’re seeing a massive influx,” Dweck said. “Bigger brands are leaning in far more and have been a bit looser with brand guidelines in terms of the content we’ll accept and publish. Alongside that, we’re trying to negotiate as many direct deals for distribution rights for the creative assets we’re getting from creators. We’re seeing a 40% to 60% uplift against typical, traditionally produced creative units, mainly on TikTok, but the uplift is similar across Instagram and YouTube.”

Retail media networks are becoming another key channel for creator partnerships, according to [Modern Retail’s 2026 guide to creator marketing](https://www.modernretail.co/marketing/modern-retail-research-the-marketers-2026-guide-to-creator-marketing-with-duolingo-ulta-and-youtube/). Seventeen percent of respondents to Modern Retail’s first-quarter survey said they are partnering with influencers to create content for retail media — making it the second most used media channel for creator-brand partnerships after social media (96%).

The convergence of creator marketing and retail media is increasingly being formalized through data partnerships, including Omnicom Media’s [agreement](https://digiday.com/media-buying/at-ces-omnicom-media-ties-a-deal-with-walmart-purchase-data-into-metas-influencer-followers/) with Meta to connect Walmart Connect purchase data with Instagram creator campaigns, allowing marketers to better connect influencer activity with sales outcomes. The company struck a similar agreement with TikTok the previous year, underscoring growing demand from advertisers for more measurable creator marketing programs.

When Modern Retail asked survey respondents about their goals for working with creators, the top five responses were community building (61%), paid media amplification and branded content creation (tied at 57%), building authenticity (50%) and establishing expertise and authority (46%).

Go Fish Digital’s Dweck sees creator partnerships as an opportunity to produce authentic, platform-native content that can drive consumers further down the funnel. “I look at influencers for reach versus creators for content creation and a higher volume of assets that look and feel far more lifelike than the typical ads that advertisers are pushing out,” he said. “Creators live a bit more down funnel. It’s taking $100,000 and spreading it across a handful of creators versus trying to spend that on one or two influencers that are going to have mass reach and appeal, but may not drive the bottom line results you’re hoping for.”

Leveraging creators with smaller followings can help UGC feel more authentic. These programs can also offer more consistent touch points, as brands can push out prompts to hundreds or thousands of micro- and mid-creators rather than having to reach out to larger creators to organize specific campaigns.

“Creator marketing is becoming much more community-driven,” Stacey McCormick, CMO at Aerie, told Digiday in June 2026. “Creators are especially responding to the sense of access and community feeling like they’re genuinely part of the brand ecosystem rather than just participating in a campaign.”

The executives Modern Retail spoke with for this report said that their clients primarily work with creators to build trust and establish authentic relationships.

“In all of the client conversations that I’ve had at least for this year, the idea of trust has come up most frequently, and the idea that you can use creators and influencers to piggyback off of that existing audience, and \[build\] trust for your own brand has been something that is especially appealing,” said Harry Browne, vp of TV, audio and display innovation at Tinuiti.

Against the backdrop of Advertising Week New York this week, the programmatic ecosystem has been buzzing madly like the inhabitants of an overturned beehive.

That’s because Apple’s latest operating system update, iOS 27, which launched in mid-September, has been, without warning, unconditionally blocking data and identity vendors. The original list included LiveRamp, Permutive, Audigent (now owned by Experian) and the Unified ID 2.0 program, as well as [The Trade Desk’s adsrvr.org](https://www.adexchanger.com/platforms/apples-latest-operating-system-blocks-the-trade-desk-from-serving-ads-on-safari/), its root domain for serving ads.

Earlier this week, Apple released a new WebKit beta – iOS 27.2, for those keeping track – that removes The Trade Desk’s adsrvr.org from the blocklist, which is, phew, good news for TTD.

But this doesn’t mean the overarching problem is solved.

[As AdExchanger reported](https://www.adexchanger.com/privacy/apple-has-far-reaching-plans-to-block-hundreds-of-programmatic-data-companies-from-ios/) after conversations with sources who have knowledge of the WebKit group’s plans, Apple is devising a far more expansive potential blocklist list that would include hundreds of ad tech, mar tech and identity vendors that handle user data and device IDs.

AdExchanger has now spoken with most of the known principals involved in the story (as in, the companies blocked by iOS 27) as well as with others working closely with the Apple WebKit group, although no Apple exec or insider has responded to requests for comment.

Here is what we learned.

**The TTD fix**

The first and most visible casualty of Apple’s iOS 27 surprise was The Trade Desk.

But after weeks of uncertainty, WebKit’s ad tech leader John Wilander [informed](https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=324771) The Trade Desk engineering’s leader Ian Meyers of the iOS 27.2 beta, which removes adsrvr.org from the blocklist.

Although this is good news for TTD, it must wait for iOS 27.2 to become the live install version of iOS, which might not happen for three or four weeks. If you download the new iOS 27 today, it will still block TTD’s ads from serving.

Luckily, the install rate for iOS 27 is still relatively low and the timeline short enough that this will only be a revenue blip for a company of TTD’s size. But the bigger relief is that there’s no need to undergo a costly migration to a new ad-serving domain.

In retrospect, the block seemed aimed at match.adsrvr.org, TTD’s cookie-sync endpoint. But Safari blocks at the domain level, so it took out the core ad-serving domain, too. When TTD was founded, keeping everything under one domain meant better match rates and faster ad serving, and no one was worried about browsers blocking by domain. Now, with the rise of privacy-by-default standards and crackdowns on cross-device tracking, TTD probably wishes it had put matching on a separate domain entirely.

**What about the rest of us?**

Still, for The Trade Desk at least, this probably feels like a major potential crisis averted. Adsrvr.org lives to serve another day.

But the core issue has not been resolved. As several measurement vendors pointed out unprompted during Advertising Week gatherings, the initial focus on The Trade Desk has obscured how big of a deal – and bad – this iOS update is for analytics and attribution.

Marketers rely on LiveRamp, UID2 and other still-blocked identity providers and identifiers for cross-channel matching. They need identity to stitch streaming media placements with mobile ads and web traffic, for example, or to connect TV spots with spikes in organic search.

Well, sayonara to that.

In addition, data and identity vendors commonly insert alternative IDs in the bidstream for Safari ads because third-party cookies and other identifiers have been removed. Many DSPs only bid for targetable placements, so vendors need to add an ID of some kind.

Goodbye to that tactic as well.

And then there’s the relatively minor but extremely thorny issue of advertisers that paid for iOS 27 ads that didn’t render.

As two agency ad buyers told AdExchanger on background, the win logs for their customers that use TTD contain ads for iOS 27 that clearly did not serve. In other words, those brands *won* auctions and paid for ads no one saw. Other impressions were targeted using LiveRamp’s RampID, which derives from the blocked pippio.com domain.

Fortunately, iOS 27’s user base is still small, and ad buying systems can route spend elsewhere, so the losses are limited. But some money did go to ads that never rendered.

Which raises the question: Do advertisers get paid back?

Whether an advertiser can contractually recoup its spend is based on the cascade of relationships between publishers, SSPs, DSPs and advertisers, according to two execs at companies directly involved.

So enjoy that reconciliation process.

**Apple’s POV**

Meanwhile, Apple has been characteristically unresponsive.

Sure, The Trade Desk’s Meyers and Apple’s Wilander had a [back-and-forth on WebKit Bugzilla](https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=324771), which also alludes to a separate email exchange. But those interactions appear to be the extent of Apple’s communications on the iOS 27 blocklist matter.

Not that Apple is ever chatty about policy changes. But this time it’s even less forthcoming than usual.

According to multiple leaders at blocked companies who spoke with AdExchanger on the condition of anonymity, this iOS 27 update stands in stark contrast to Apple’s Intelligent Tracking Prevention for WebKit, the first version of which was released with iOS 11 in 2017. It’s also a different beast than when Apple’s AppTrackingTransparency policy went live with iOS 14 in 2021.

In both cases, AdExchanger’s sources said, Apple released guidance and public statements, and held sessions about the changes during its developer conference.

This time, the blocked companies were left to figure it out themselves, usually after a publisher client or partner asked why ads had stopped rendering. One engineering leader compared it to a heart attack: “Very subtle, easy-to-ignore signals, then all of a sudden.”

Boom.

Then again, one publisher ad tech exec who works with the WebKit group argued that secrecy is the point. The WebKit team can’t trust ad tech, the exec said, so it purposely keeps the blocklist’s rules and workings hidden.

Permutive, for instance, the publisher noted, simply rotated to a new domain shortly after discovering “permutive.com” had been blocked.

# How Amazon Fall Prime Day went for sellers

Once again, Amazon’s fall Prime Big Deals Days event kicked off the holiday shopping season early.

The fall sale, held from October 6 to 7, helped drive major online sales growth across categories like electronics, apparel, beauty and even household essentials. As price-conscious consumers continue to seek out discounts and bundled deals, Amazon sellers and rival retailers have adapted their promotional strategies to capture early holiday demand.

According to Adobe Analytics tracking, U.S. retailers drove $9.86 billion in online sales from October 6 to 7, representing 8.5% growth year over year. That’s up from 7.3% growth between 2024 and 2025. Adobe’s report pointed to this pattern as having “changed the shape of the holiday shopping season, pushing U.S. retailers to manage promotions and inventory effectively to capture an additional pre-season spike in shopping interest.”

At the category level, online sales across U.S. retailers were driven by electronics, up 85% compared to average daily sales in September 2026. Meanwhile, toys jumped 158%, video games rose 90%, and personal care rose 73%.

When it comes to specific products, Adobe data shows shoppers used deals to stock up on essentials, with sales of household cleaning and paper products up 55% year over year, personal hygiene products up 45% and pet food up 45%.

Notably, apparel basics were up 25% year over year, according to Adobe. That momentum appears to build on the summer’s Prime Day event, when apparel [overtook](https://www.numerator.com/prime-day/) home and gardens as one of the top categories in the U.S. and globally, according to Numerator.

Indeed, fashion sellers on Amazon are seeing pleasantly positive results despite overall weakness across the category this year.

Minsun Yoo, founder of hat maker Ponyflo, said that Amazon Prime Big Deal Days was “a strong event” for the brand. “Sales came in 40% above our goal, exceeding the sales from last year’s event,” Yoo said, with this healthy momentum boding well for the start of the holiday shopping season. The brand offered 20% off its signature caps.

“Overall, this year’s event is showing a meaningfully stronger sales lift than last year, despite a more cautious promotional environment across the category,” Yoo said.

## **Enticing price-conscious shoppers** 

Evan Feldstein, general manager of Foreo North America, said this year’s event brought price-sensitive customers to the beauty tech brand.

Feldstein did not share exact revenue figures, but said sales are up 16% year over year from last year’s Big Deals Days event. When it comes to consumer behavior during Amazon Big Deals Days, Feldstein said it was “unusually price sensitive this year,” compared to prior years.

“Our Luna fourth generation was our biggest seller this year by revenue and volume,” Feldstein. This was somewhat unexpected as the facial cleansing device is the brand’s entry-level product, retailing for $99 and offered at 40% off during the fall Prime Day sale. Foreo’s other devices, like the popular Bear series, typically range from $199-$399. The brand offered various discounts depending on the SKU during fall Prime Day.

## **Driving discovery through bundles** 

Value was another big draw for customers during this year’s fall Prime Day.

K-Beauty brand Gemi, known for its Hand Sanitizer + Serum hero product, had a strong opening on fall Prime Day, generating more than three times its typical daily Amazon sales.

Gemi co-founder Erin Choi said shoppers came ready to stock up, with average order value up nearly 50% from past Prime Day sales.

Sales were fueled by strong demand for Gemi’s sets, like curated fragrance trios and the brand’s five-scent Classic collection. The company offered 20% off on these sets of three- and five-scent bundles. Sets and trios accounted for nearly 70% of Gemi’s opening-day sales, which Choi said showed customers took advantage of the deals to discover a broader sampling of Gemi’s fragrance collection, rather than purchasing individual scents.

Gemi co-founder Hau Yeung said the company’s strategy of creating multiple curated trios across its six signature fragrances has paid off. Yeung said the results validate Gemi’s overall strategy of offering customers a “fragrance wardrobe” of elevated hand care rather than just a functional sanitizer.

“The performance of these curated sets also signals promising demand for discovery and gifting formats heading into the holiday season,” Choi said.

ChatGPT visibility and conversions are strongly correlated. A joint study by Profound, [Kevin Indig](https://www.linkedin.com/in/kevinindig/), and [Eric Van Buskirk](https://www.linkedin.com/in/vanbuskirk/) of Clickstream Solutions watched 56 people compare products inside ChatGPT across 221 real tasks, then matched what they chose against Profound's data on which brands ChatGPT actually cites. It is one of the first behavioral links between AI visibility and what people pick.

The brands participants chose appeared about twice as often in ChatGPT's answers as the ones they passed over (24% share of voice against 11%). Visibility and choice correlate strongly at 0.57 and 92.8% of tasks ended with no click to the open web!

Inside ChatGPT, share of voice is shelf space. And shelf space predicts the sale.

### [**Share of voice predicts conversions**](#share-of-voice-predicts-conversions)

Shoppers act on whatever ChatGPT presents to them. The more a brand shows up when someone asks about a category, the more likely that brand gets chosen. Across categories, that relationship holds at a correlation of 0.57.

The link is strong but not deterministic. It runs as high as 0.87 in pet insurance and 0.97 in grocery, then collapses to 0.13 in meal delivery, a category with enough brands to trust the number. A few heavily cited brands still lost..

One boundary is worth stating plainly. What the study measured is share of voice, how often a brand appears across answers, not its rank inside a given section. ChatGPT returns many sections per answer with only a few citations in most, so citation rank within a section sits outside what this data can claim. Citation rank could be counted via the right-rail results panel, but those ordinal “ranks” are not useful since they’re not split by section. Visibility matters most when the shopper knows little about the category. Prior category knowledge was low or medium in 88% of tasks. When a shopper arrives without a preferred brand, the model's shortlist becomes the map, and visibility does the most work exactly there.

The link is strong in most categories, though coaching (-0.98) and fitness apps (-0.44) reverse it, likely noise given how few brands sit in each.

*Table 2. See Appendix A to see the sample sizes for each brand*

### [**Unknown brands can instill curiosity**](#unknown-brands-can-instill-curiosity)

When ChatGPT named a brand a participant had never heard of, curiosity spiked and the brand often survived to the final shortlist. "*I've actually never heard of Misfits Market, and I am super interested*," one participant said. Another: "*both services I didn't know existed before this study*".

The jump from first exposure to active comparison happened inside a single sentence. "*I've never done pet insurance. I do have a dog, so that would be interesting to me. Now help me find pet insurance.*" One prompt, and a cold category turned into a live decision.

Presentation decided which newcomers survived. **Top-listed options drew more attention and more text, a clear "best for" label gave the shopper a reason, and a plausible price sealed it**. Lower-ranked options lost for a structural reason too: the model hands them less to work with. "*The less information I get, it feels like they give up on the lower options*," one participant said.

The only reliable killers were price, poor fit and a disclosed downside. Unfamiliarity almost never did the damage. That is the opening for a challenger. A brand nobody has heard of can win the shortlist in one session, as long as the model lists it and frames it well.

The catch: the study pushed participants to "pick two" in the task, which nudged people toward finalizing, and the sample is small. Read near-universal curiosity as strong inside the study and directional outside it.

### [**The decision happens without a click**](#the-decision-happens-without-a-click)

Clicks barely happen. 92.8% of *all tasks* ended with no meaningful click to the open web, and 3.2% verified a claim on an outside site. No participant cross-checked a single price externally! Eight participants clicked out during their entire study; nine clicked out two to three times.

Checking did happen, but it stayed inside the chat. **Almost half of tasks, 48.9%, ended with the shopper accepting the named options and no follow-up at all**. When people did push, they asked ChatGPT to justify itself, 38.8% of tasks, far more often than they opened a new tab. The verification talk was aspirational. Participants said they would go read Reddit, then mostly did not.

For a marketer, the meaning is uncomfortable because analytics will never track this. No click means no referral session and no last touch to attribute, so **referral and click-through reports undercount the channel by design**. It also means no correction step. Nobody lands on your site to discover the real price or the feature ChatGPT left out, so whatever the model says stands as fact. The work moves off your website and into the answer itself.

*Table 4. See Appendix B for confidence intervals*

Assessable base of 219 tasks, with N/A excluded. Together, 93.6% were comparing or decision-ready, and none ended overwhelmed or without a next step.

### [**The comparison grid is the decision surface**](#the-comparison-grid-is-the-decision-surface)

A grid is the comparison table ChatGPT builds when you ask it to weigh options: brands down the side, attributes across the top, price and "best for" and key features in the cells. Options sit side by side, and the shopper reads across.

That grid is where people choose products. Working from screen recordings, annotators coded which on-screen element held attention longest in each task. After the plain answer text, the grid won. Brand and product grids dominated 35.9% of tasks and feature grids another 15.0%, more than any other structured element. In 65.4% of tasks, people scanned rather than read closely

They loved it. "*These tables are epic.*" "*This table format makes it easier to scan through the differences quickly instead of reading long reviews.*" Several learned to prompt for a grid outright! One kept using a grid after seeing it was incomplete: "*So this isn't even a full complete chart, which is not great. But this helps me the most, so I'm going to continue going off of these*".

For an unfamiliar brand, the "best for" label and the price cell stood in for everything the shopper did not know. Your row is your shelf placement. Whether you appear, what label you carry, and what price sits beside you settle the comparison before the shopper forms an opinion. Clean specs, named use cases, and a current price are what put a brand in the grid. **Getting lifted into that table is the AEO equivalent of owning a featured snippet.**

After the plain answer, the grid held attention more than any other element, and users scanned it. Mean task time was 236 seconds.

The SEO industry has spent the last few months taking ChatGPT apart to see how it searches and finds its sources.

We wanted to see for ourselves how ChatGPT retrieves information—and what that means for AI visibility—so we analyzed 66.6 million free, logged-out GPT-5.6 Luna responses and their 15 million fan-out queries from August and September.

Sidenote

Free sessions are closer to how most people use ChatGPT: more than 90% of its weekly users are on the free plan, according to [Olivier de Segonzac](https://fr.linkedin.com/in/resoneo/fr), co-founder of [RESONEO](https://www.resoneo.com/), in [Search Engine Land](https://searchengineland.com/inside-chatgpt-search-web-run-fan-out-queries-ai-visibility-477339).

Logging out also strips out chat history and memory, so we see ChatGPT's default behavior rather than answers shaped by one person's past chats.

`site:` operator to search a single website, spread across \~116K different domains.
Only 14.4% of the 66.6 million ChatGPT responses we tracked triggered a web search.

When ChatGPT did search, it ran an average of about 1.6 fan-out queries for each response that searched.

Every web search costs OpenAI money, so it makes sense for ChatGPT to skip one when it can answer well enough from what it already knows.

This fits with [WordLift's research](https://wordlift.io/blog/en/ai-free-tiers-comparison/) which found that free-tier style models may lean more on training data to keep costs down.

This means that, for many prompts, your chances of appearing depend on what ChatGPT already knows about your brand, rather than what it can find.

Of the 15 million fan-outs we analyzed, 6.8% used the `site:` operator to search a single website.

And among the \~160 most-searched sites, three in four of those searches targeted a brand site.

By "brand site," we mean a company website like apple.com or ikea.com, as opposed to a retailer, government site, forum, or review site.

Retailers like Walmart, Costco and Amazon made up 11.9%, and Reddit and Facebook just 1.9% between them.

The words inside the fan-outs show the same focus on official, first-hand information, with “official” and “price” the most common after “2026”, and growing by a few percentage points month-over-month.

None of this is a big surprise. If you want a product’s price or specifications, a brand site is the obvious place to check.

When a question has no single right answer, that’s when ChatGPT is more likely to look beyond official sources.

For instance, in a separate test of 20,000 US prompts, 84.4% of factual questions about pricing, product features or company details cited **at least one** official source.

For comparison questions like “A vs B” or “which is cheaper”, that dropped to 68.3%.

The mix of sources changed too.

For factual questions, 63.4% of citations were to official websites.

For comparison questions, it was 46.4%, so most citations went to other sites.

So ChatGPT relies most on official sources for facts, and leans more on other sites when it has to weigh one option against another.

We’ll dive deeper into fan-out query language a little later.

Make sure your brand site can answer the factual questions

If ChatGPT is going to run `site:youbrand.com` searches for your prices, specs and support details, those facts need to be on your site, in plain text, on a page it can find.

The domains ChatGPT targets most with `site:` are big consumer brands.

These rankings are, of course, based on our own dataset and prompts, but with around 1 million `site:` queries behind them, they give a strong sense of which domains ChatGPT leans on most.

These are mostly brands that sell products, so a brand site is the natural source for details like prices and specs.

Government domains also feature heavily.

Gov.br, gov.uk, France’s service-public.fr, the NHTSA, the FDA and the SEC all sit in the top 150, which matches [the observations](https://lilyraynyc.substack.com/p/what-we-can-learn-from-evolving-chatgpt) of [Lily Ray](https://www.linkedin.com/in/lily-ray-44755615), Founder of [Algorythmic](https://algorythmic.co/), that ChatGPT favors official sources for YMYL questions.

Note also that Reddit is still the ninth most `site:` searched domain.

This fits with [the findings](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/suganthan-mohanadasan_chatgpt-searched-a-specific-subreddit-by-activity-7497911316712632320-8DCt) of [Suganthan Mohanadasan](https://ae.linkedin.com/in/suganthan-mohanadasan), co-founder of [Snippet Digital](https://snippet.digital/), that ChatGPT still fetches Reddit when it wants real users’ opinions, despite citing it less often (which we’ll get to later).

Of the 17 publishers and platforms that currently have [licensing deals with OpenAI](https://tenpointlabs.com/post/ai-publisher-licensing-deals-brand-visibility-in-ai-search), Reddit is the only one in the top 150 most `site:` searched domains.

One possible reason is that ChatGPT already has its partner content pre-loaded and ready to go.

Those `site:` searches show what ChatGPT looks up during query fan-out, but not what it ends up citing.

The cited domains tell a different story. Partner publications are everywhere.

In Brand Radar, partner titles among ChatGPT’s 200 most-cited domains more than doubled their combined share of citations, from 7.5% in March to 15.8% in July—and still held 12.5% in late September.

It's worth trying to get your brand coverage in [these partner publications](https://tenpointlabs.com/post/ai-publisher-licensing-deals-brand-visibility-in-ai-search), because ChatGPT is citing them increasingly often.

The terms ChatGPT adds to its fan-out queries hint at the page types it wants to retrieve.

Between August and September, more of ChatGPT's fan-out queries were about prices, product specifications, and reviews, and slightly fewer were about definitions.

A gain of 1 or 2 percentage points can sound small, but these terms all started from a low base, and their relative rise shows starker growth.

For instance, "Price" went from 6.04% to 8.88% of fan-outs, a relative rise of nearly half (47%) in one month.

Adding to this, "Reviews" grew by a third, and "specifications" entered the top 50 for the first time.

On the flip side, "Meaning" and "definition" each fell by about a fifth, though from small shares, so that’s likely a dip rather than a trend.

You can assess which fan-out query types are most prominent in your industry using Brand Radar.

*Thi*s [*story*](https://digiday.com/marketing/ruggables-new-ad-spend-strategy-shifts-focus-to-shopmy-creators/) *was originally published by Modern Retail’s sister site, [Digiday](https://digiday.com/).*

The direct-to-consumer playbook was built on performance — spend big on Meta and cash in on the conversion. But as digital ad costs rise and performance dwindles, DTC darling Ruggable is tearing up that playbook.

“We have been focused on shifting over the last 18 months is a classic: what got us here is not going to get us there,” Lauren Sherman-Kaoud, chief marketing and creative officer at Ruggable, told Digiday.

Since last August, Ruggable has shifted about 10% of its overall spend from performance channels, like Meta, into brand channels, like influencers and connected television. The brand plans to grow that spend by another 15% to 20% next year, Sherman-Kaoud said. The CMO declined to offer a specific dollar figure for its marketing budget.

“We don’t really need to be showing up in the bottom-of-funnel affiliate networks, when ShopMy is working so well as a conversion channel for us,” she said.

Influencer marketing used to be managed by a small team overseeing direct messages and spreadsheets. That’s now run by a single person, and those overhead costs have since been reallocated to Ruggable’s marketing mix, Sherman-Kaoud told Digigday. She did not disclose specific dollar figures.

In working directly with creators through ShopMy, Ruggable’s working media has outperformed traditional ads, and even TikTok as a conversion channel, said Sherman-Kaoud. The brand saw roughly $3 million in revenue the first month of its ShopMy partnership, the CMO added. That figure doubled the following month and tripled in month three.

Influencer marketing efforts started last holiday shopping season. Ruggable took upwards of a million dollars out of its performance budget — specifically from Meta — and pumped that spend into ShopMy creators, said Sherman-Kaoud.

The washable rug brand has a two-pronged approach to its creator marketing strategy — affiliate marketers for scale and conversion, and brand ambassadors for things like product collaborations or bigger activations.

Across ShopMy, Ruggable works with hundreds of creators, mostly in an affiliate capacity. The brand sets parameters around post format, content volume and which product will be promoted. Other than that, “we let them do their thing,” the CMO said. On the brand ambassador side, creators act as spokespeople for the brand, providing a “halo to the brand,” she said. The DTC has partnered with high-profiles like food personality Dan Pelosi and Spread the Jelly media company.

“It’s sort of like a sandwich approach a little bit,” Sherman-Kaoud said. “We’ve got a massive investment there \[in brand marketing\], and then we use ShopMy to replace some of those worst-performing affiliate channels.”

If it sounds like traditional advertising, that’s because it is. Companies take a similar approach to media, negotiating deals with big players like Disney or Walmart while buying ads across long tail players programmatically.

Ruggable may be ahead of the curb, according to Noah Eisemann, global executive director of creator and influencer at VML. More brands, however, are starting to think of their creator strategies more holistically.

“People are just discovering efficiencies and just waking up,” Eisemann said.

Ruggable is on track to IPO over the next three years, making brand awareness a crucial part of its marketing strategy, per Sherman-Kaoud. Ruggable is in the early stages of developing an internal ambassador program to build long term relationships with interior designers and other related creators.

Call it a matter of maturity. Early on, influencers were an earned media, PR play, he added. Now, brands are layering in performance with affiliate creators, ultimately boosting brand awareness without sacrificing sales and conversion.

It’s not a bifurcated approach, per se, according to Eisemann. “It’s just that they’re thinking about their strategy holistically and understanding that there’s different levers and tactics and scale to pull respective to the business objectives that they’re setting for themselves.”

Prime time is coming to the feed.

On Thursday, Meta announced a new feature, called Ads Super Burst, that lets advertisers lock in a window of between three and 24 hours on a single day across Facebook and Instagram, such as during the Grammys or opening weekend of the new NBA season.

The price and approximate reach are agreed up front.

If that sounds a lot like how broadcasters sell their inventory, well, that’s the idea.

Advertisers pick the slot, and Meta commits to generate a specific amount of reach, within 5% of a set forecast. In the US, brands can even reserve category exclusivity on select tentpole dates so no rival gets the same window.

The tool is now generally available and it’s something advertisers have been asking for, according to Simon Whitcombe, VP of Meta’s global business group for North America.

“Advertisers have always looked for ways to buy certainty for their biggest moments,” he said, “and, increasingly, they want that certainty where attention actually is.”

## **The 24-hour upfront**

But for all of that, this isn’t quite a traditional reserved buy, according to Whitcombe.

Beyond just securing inventory, Super Burst is also about buying “a share of a defined audience,” he said, “with frequency fixed at one so every impression reaches a different person.”

Pricing is the other big difference. Standard reach campaigns are bought in the auction, so CPMs rise and fall with demand. But Super Burst CPMs vary by date. “A major cultural moment prices differently from an ordinary Tuesday,” Whitcombe said. Certainty comes with a cost.

There’s a catch, though. Inventory will be scarce depending on the date. Super Burst is available on a first come, first served basis, and even on a platform with billions of users, like Meta, the best windows could go quickly. A retailer eyeing a major shopping holiday, for example, would need to book well in advance, Whitcombe said.

But he was also quick to point out that Super Burst isn’t meant to replace anything an advertiser is already doing. “The day is a peak on top of an always-on campaign,” he said, “not a substitute for it.”

This whole pitch should ring a bell for anyone who’s bought YouTube Reserve, Google’s way of locking in YouTube inventory in advance at a fixed price. But asked about the parallel, Whitcombe demurred.

“I’ll leave comparisons with other platforms to others,” he said.

But Whitcombe did note that the product could work for both TV advertisers and digital-first brands, because “the best way to experience a lot of the largest cultural moments today is through social media and short-form video.”

## **Short videos, long memories**

Short-form video is central to Meta’s theory of brand building, which is that people buy the brands they remember.

That may sound obvious, but there are also stats to back it up. According to [WPP Media](https://www.marketingweek.com/most-purchases-consumers-primed/), 84% of purchases are made by shoppers who already had a brand in mind before they started shopping.

Meta, naturally, sees its own apps as fertile ground for forming memories and brand associations, especially through the consumption of short-form video. According to Whitcombe, short-form makes up roughly half of all time spent with media in general, and Reels alone is responsible for more than half of all time spent on Instagram.

He sorts Meta’s brand-focused tools into two related buckets: those that build memory and those that reinforce it.

Super Burst belongs in the “memory building” bucket, according to Whitcombe, alongside another tool that Meta announced on Thursday called First Impression Ads, still in early alpha testing, which gives brands a chance to buy the first ad someone sees when they open the Facebook app. (You’d be forgiven if [Snap comes to mind](https://www.adexchanger.com/social-media/snap-sales-svp-peter-naylor-on-upstart-competition-why-snap-avoids-exchanges-and-the-wide-release-of-first-commercial/), since it’s had a product with a similar name and the same idea since roughly 2020.)

And then there’s Aggregated View Time, a new video metric, also teased on Thursday and now in early testing, that measures short-form video by adding up the time someone spends with a brand over the course of a week rather than simply counting the views. That falls in the “reinforcing memory” bucket, Whitcombe said.

According to Meta’s internal research, five seconds of attention spread over a week can drive 32% more offline sales than one continuous five-second view.

“This is about consistency,” Whitcombe said, “being distinctive and repeated week after week so you stay top of mind long before anyone is shopping.”

# An intelligent new shopping cart

As we build for the future of commerce, our focus spans two fronts: unlocking agentic capabilities that act on your behalf, and designing practical tools that give shoppers confidence and control. Google’s Universal Cart is built for that second track — mirroring how people actually shop today across Google, without losing track of their items, their savings, or the merchants they trust.

The [Universal Cart](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/products/shopping/google-shopping-cart/), which we previewed earlier this year, is an intelligent shopping cart and your new hub for shopping on Google. The cart puts you in control, helping to organize your shopping, keep track of items you love from across retailers, stay on top of promos, and enjoy effortless checkout powered by the Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP). Today, Universal Cart is rolling out in the U.S. across Google Search and in the Gemini app.

## The cart for all your shopping

Here are four things the new Universal Cart lets you do to stay organized and shop more confidently this holiday season.

**1. Save products from multiple retailers, wherever you’re shopping on Google.** Universal Cart offers a more organized alternative to tabs and screenshots. The cart saves your progress across Google so you never have to start your shopping from scratch. Let’s say you save a handbag from Steve Madden to your cart in [AI Mode in Search](http://g.ai/), and later a sweater from Quince and lipgloss from Ulta Beauty in the Gemini app. Those products will be there in your cart when you come back later so you can pick up right where you left off.

**2. Keep tabs on pricing or inventory changes for your entire list.** The cart is built on the 60+ billion continually refreshed product listings in Google’s Shopping Graph. This allows it to proactively work for you in the background, sending notifications about price drops or when an item comes back in stock.

**3. Identify hidden savings or points from your cart.** The cart’s intelligent reasoning can help anticipate your needs. Say you have a couple different credit cards, but don’t know each one’s specific benefits. The Universal Cart is built on Google Wallet so it understands your card perks and can intelligently help you choose between payment methods. It’ll also show you relevant promo codes right from the cart.

**4. Make seamless, trusted purchases when you’re ready to buy.** In online shopping, trust is everything. You can securely check out with Google Pay in just a few taps with many of your favorite stores right in the cart, or you can transfer your items directly to the merchant’s cart to finish buying on their site. Try these simplified checkout experiences with merchants like Nike, Sephora, Target, Ulta Beauty, Walmart, Wayfair, and many Shopify merchants. Either way, you will receive direct confirmations and customer support from the merchant, and they will remain the seller of record.

As the holiday season kicks into high gear, the Universal Cart is just one way we’re giving shoppers the convenience and smarts they need to make the best shopping choices.

Ad industry insiders [have](https://www.adexchanger.com/data-driven-thinking/ai-slop-is-the-new-mfa-and-we-all-need-to-fight-it/) consistently [warned](https://www.adexchanger.com/data-driven-thinking/ai-is-bringing-mfa-to-social-media-heres-how-advertisers-can-avoid-it/) that generative AI would ignite [an explosion in made-for-advertising (MFA) sites](https://www.adexchanger.com/ai/mfa-ad-spend-is-increasing-is-ai-slop-to-blame/) that cynically monetize via programmatic ad tech.

Well, research is starting to prove the case.

A [study](https://decryptads.com/blog/posts/ai-recipe-slop-networks.html) released Tuesday by advertising supply chain intelligence company DecryptAds uncovered more than 2,100 AI-generated recipe sites that take a page straight out of the [MFA playbook,](https://www.adexchanger.com/publishers/inside-the-secret-meetings-to-define-mfa/) with multiple overlapping ad placements crammed onto pages filled by low-effort content. DecryptAds found ads from major blue chip and Fortune 500 brands appearing on these recipe sites.

The report examines sites populated by AI-generated recipes, although the same publishers operate all sorts of other ad-supported sites, such as political news aggregators and car, anime and video game forums.

By examining ads.txt and sellers.json files, DecryptAds determined that the recipe sites appear to be monetized by SSPs that work with ad tech partners located in what DecryptAds refers to as “risky geos.” These “risky geos” are associated with high degrees of cybercrime or often have adversarial relationships with the US, according to Zach Edwards, co-founder and chief of product and research at DecryptAds.

The idea that US citizens – including, potentially, government officials – can access these sites, have their data harvested by ad tech vendors and possibly be targeted with malvertising schemes presents major cybersecurity concerns, Edwards told AdExchanger. However, he noted that DecryptAds has not uncovered evidence of any crimes committed by these sites or their ad tech partners.

Regardless, the ad inventory on the sites is of dubious value, Edwards said. Just like with MFA, the sites are packed to the gills with ad placements designed to game viewability.

They duplicate viral recipe trends or copy popular pages from other cooking sites to produce close-enough versions that were clearly not reviewed by a person. The sites sometimes feature crazy foods that only make sense as a bucket of search keywords (“[Hot Cocoa Buffalo Chicken Gingerbread Dip with Marshmallow Topping](https://defector.com/glossy-gunky-and-ready-in-minutes-ai-meal-recipes-are-overrunning-the-internet), anyone?”)

But to anyone with eyes, it should be clear that these sites have no place in a healthy programmatic supply chain, Edwards said, especially in light of recent Google Search changes that deprioritize sites featuring AI-generated authors and creators.

But whether to serve ads on such sites is a choice that many SSPs are still grappling with.

## **AI avatars**

Part of what makes these sites hard to police is that they’re built to look like the work of real people.

The networks of sites uncovered by DecryptAds feature fabricated authors on their “about” pages. These author profiles often include AI-generated human avatars, or in some cases, stock images, stolen pictures of real chefs and even slightly altered images of celebrities like actress Emily Blunt.

These sites rarely disclose that their authors are not real people, which means they run afoul of a [Google helpful content update](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) rolled out just this month.

The new Google Search policy states that “fabricating creator profiles (such as by using AI-generated headshots, made-up names or false credentials to make content appear as if it was written by human experts) is a form of deception. Any form of deception makes a page untrustworthy to both users and our automated quality systems, and is a signal of a low-quality page.”

According to Edwards, the advertising industry should take Google’s new policy as a sign that if websites don’t disclose their use of AI-generated authors, then the publishers and their vendors risk being officially classified as “low-quality” and therefore unfit for monetization.

But according to a source at an SSP who spoke with AdExchanger on background in exchange for candor, the Google guidance only applies to Google’s search business and should therefore be treated separately from best practices suggested by Google Ads.

This source also disputed the premise that sites featuring AI-generated authors have no inherent value for advertisers or audiences. After all, real people click those links and engage with AI-generated content all the time, they said.

## **The DecryptAds methodology**

But quibbling over philosophical questions about AI avatars and bylines is arguably beside the point.

After all, the issue appeared on the DecryptAds team’s radar, Edwards said, because of concerns about potential cybercrimes and state-backed bad-actors exploiting the ad supply chain.

It’s worth reiterating that the report does not contain evidence of any crimes committed by the sites or their ad tech partners, Edwards said. The operators appear less like sophisticated threat actors than opportunists running a low-effort content-farm playbook.

But cybersecurity concerns did inform the methodology used by DecryptAds. The team first discovered the more than 2,100 recipe sites covered in the report during its regular monitoring of ad tech companies registered in what they consider “risky geos,” Edwards said.

Think Russia, China, Cyprus, Turkey and the United Arab Emirates. These nations, Edwards said, are either under direct US sanctions, have an adversarial relationship with the US, maintain little to no privacy firewall between the government and tech companies or have associations with high degrees of cybercrime and ad fraud. DecryptAds groups these nations into threat tiers, with US-sanctioned nations like Russia in the top tier.

DecryptAds started by examining the supply chains of about 300 ad tech companies based in these risky geos, Edwards said, eventually deriving a list of publishers working with those 300 companies. It got this data by looking at ads.txt files. DecryptAds also determined which SSPs work with those 300 ad tech companies by examining the sellers.json files maintained by the SSPs, as well as by looking at domain name system (DNS) data, SSL certificates and Google Analytics data.

Using a list of food-related keywords, Edwards narrowed the list of sites monetized by the 300 ad tech companies to an initial list of “400 suspicious recipe websites,” he said. Over the past few years there has been a [dramatic increase](https://digiday.com/media/were-seeing-an-immense-uplift-in-the-scale-how-generative-ai-is-fueling-the-next-wave-of-ad-tech-fraud/) in websites publishing content written with AI who monetize their sites with online ads, and AI recipe websites have likely been one of the fastest growing niches. These sites have been [diverting advertiser budgets](https://www.adexchanger.com/ai/mfa-ad-spend-is-increasing-is-ai-slop-to-blame/) from many legacy publishers and [wasting ad spends](https://www.adweek.com/media/ai-slop-is-fooling-advertisers-verification-tools/). In this report alone we found ads from brands including Adobe, HBO Max, Siemens, Subaru, The Wall Street Journal, Capital One, Sam’s Club, LinkedIn, Google Workspace, Tumi, Pepsi, Anker and VRBO running on these sites.

It’s also become common knowledge that publishers in certain niches are being openly deceptive about their owners and authors, using AI photos and fake back stories on their sites. Many of these sites are also aggressively [spreading their AI slop on social media sites like Pinterest](https://futurism.com/pinterest-ai-slop) with the hopes of attracting new readers.

Some sites are more aggressive, like a likely AI recipe website addcakes\[.\]com who appears to use AI generated photos of actor Emily Blunt on their website and social media profiles, claiming it’s a person named “Elena” who is “a busy mom who wanted to connect with my roots through baking, but got overwhelmed by complicated cake recipes and the pressure to make them look perfect.”

**Some of the most consistent growth in AI slop spreading across the internet has come from AI recipe websites.** Many of these are being promoted via aggressive social media accounts and there have been [numerous](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2025-11-25/ai-slop-recipes-are-taking-over-the-internet-and-thanksgiving-dinner) [articles](https://www.thecut.com/article/tiktok-ai-slop-recipe-videos-review.html) [about](https://scholarlykitchen.sspnet.org/2025/08/08/the-ai-slop-overload-does-not-taste-good/) the consumer risks from the sites and [solid](https://doubleverify.com/blog/web/verify/dv-deep-dive-serving-ai-slop-understanding-advertiser-risks-on-cooking-and-recipe-websites-with-ai-generated-content) [industry](https://deepsee.io/blog/ai-slop-sites-programmatic-advertising) [research](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/tagana-fiducia-analysis-quantifies-level-of-ai-slop-in-digital-advertising-supply-chain-for-first-time-302836519.html) highlighting the risks to advertisers’ budgets.

The “[Frankenstein recipes](https://www.npr.org/2026/01/25/nx-s1-5680290/adam-gallagher-of-food-blog-inspired-taste-discusses-the-dangers-of-ai-recipe-slop)” found on these AI recipe websites are typically being created by people not testing their recipes, so reporters investigating AI recipe slop have found recipes like “[Hot Cocoa Buffalo Chicken Gingerbread Dip with Marshmallow Topping](https://defector.com/glossy-gunky-and-ready-in-minutes-ai-meal-recipes-are-overrunning-the-internet),” which we don’t encourage anyone to actually try.

AI recipe creators have proven to not only be wasting people’s time and advertisers’ money, they can also be dangerous. A classic example was from 2023 when [a New Zealand supermarket AI app](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2023/aug/10/pak-n-save-savey-meal-bot-ai-app-malfunction-recipes) was adversarially tested and provided a recipe for ***chlorine gas*** which was described as: “the **perfect nonalcoholic beverage** to **quench your thirst** and refresh your senses.” Needless to say, that is both dangerous and ill-advised advice.

Over the past few months, the research team here at DecryptAds has been looking into how we can find AI recipe websites listed on [any of the nearly 300 ad tech companies](https://decryptads.com/geo_risk) we classify as having geographic risk, or “geo-risk” relationships  (Russia, China, corporate secrecy jurisdictions) within their ads.txt files. Our platform makes it easy to find the publishers authorizing these geo-risk-associated ad systems to monetize their websites. Once we had all that, our team was able to dive deeper into manual analysis of these sites to better understand them, their social media practices, and their ownership claims.

Most brands and businesses are trying to figure out how to improve their metrics when it comes to AI – and also what those metrics even are.

Problem is, measuring how chatbots shape brand discovery is mostly still a mystery.

But “you can’t improve what you can’t measure,” said Michael McCash, GM of growth at Australian home loan and property sales company Lendi Group.

McCash joined Lendi two years ago with a plan to sharpen the company’s more than $10 million in annual paid media, which has meant developing an in-house model for multi-touch attribution and bringing in Mutinex as its new marketing mix modeling (MMM) vendor. Lendi is also a pilot brand customer of Mutinex’s new AI measurement solution called AI Visibility.

Incorporating MMM has helped iron out wrinkles Lendi didn’t even know where there. For example, McCash said, the brand had been a major buyer of streaming TV and data-driven video on demand. Makes sense. For years, the industry has been betting on and investing in streaming as a major channel for growth.

But when Lendi dug in, what it found through its MMM reports is that old-school, free-to-air television had been “underweighted” and was actually a very efficient channel.

“We \[started\] diverting money from elsewhere in less efficient channels,” McCash said. “\[And TV\] just swallowed it up and kept increasing ROI.”

Media buyers often favor the channels they use themselves, he said, and many are young and consume a lot of streaming. Meanwhile, marketers trust the data they can easily see, meaning clicks, impressions, search term rates and other readily available metrics.

Which leads us to AI, the shiniest new marketing channel there is.

“With more people moving towards the Claudes and Geminis and ChatGPTs of the world, \[the\] initial discovery phase has become somewhat hidden again,” McCash said, like it was when Google and online search were new.

With little visibility into how AI platforms respond to prompts or surface brands, he said, many marketers are turning to information they find on forums like Reddit and X to try and piece together how people use LLMs and whether their brands show up. The platforms have made it “invisible or quite a hard task” to see how certain keywords or types of searches surface products, he added.

The Mutinex AI Visibility tool, like other AEO or GEO analytics offerings, generates insights by mass prompting LLMs with pertinent searches, like “find home loans in Western Australia,” for example, and then analyzes the results. Because there’s no reliable analytics dashboard for tracking those types of searches, the only option is to run thousands of prompts and observe the AI output.

Lendi also works with another vendor called Tracksuit that measures brand metrics and tracks how AI treats a brand compared to its competitive set. On top of that, Lendi partners with Askable for customer and mass market surveys. These tools combined help the company keep a finger on the pulse of its performance in new AI search and discovery markets.

But visibility is only part of the equation. Lendi is also testing whether advertising in AI chatbots is worth the investment.

According to McCash, the AI chatbots that include ads, such as ChatGPT and Google’s Gemini, haven’t been major ROI contributors, at least not yet.

“We’ve dipped our toes in the water,” McCash said of AI chatbot advertising. So far, though, Lendi’s MMM shows middling performance. The CPMs and customer acquisition rates are too high to justify much investment.

But what Lendi does see is a new type of customer, one who shows up to the Google search box or a Lendi-owned site having already done considerable homework on the brand. These potential home loan buyers are more knowledgeable and further down the funnel, because they’ve already done a bunch of research by prompting LLMs.

And so, for now, Lendi’s AI investment is focused less on buying chatbot ads and more on measurement and understanding how chatbots impact discovery.

McCash said he expects that the AI platforms themselves will provide more tools and help as they grow their own ad businesses, including providing data, insights and dashboards with anonymized information on the types of questions people ask and how brands show up.

Those insights are important, he said, because AI chatbots are now “the first port of call” for millions of people looking for a home or a loan. That type of data is critical for helping marketers understand how research through LLMs during the early stages can change the mindset of the customers who eventually reach them.

“All of that pre-work is being done early and in-platform now,” McCash said of AI chatbot users researching home loans. “And I think \[getting access to\] that knowledge is the next frontier” for marketers.

# Nearly 30% of holiday budgets expected to be spent by the end of October

*Below is the latest edition of Modern Retail’s Supply Chain Weekly newsletter, which goes out on Mondays at 10 a.m. ET, and dives into all things logistics and supply chain during a tumultuous time for the retail industry. To receive this weekly in your inbox*, [*click here*](https://www.modernretail.co/form/supply-chain-briefing/).

A new report from [Deloitte](https://www.deloitte.com/us/en/insights/industry/retail-distribution/holiday-retail-sales-consumer-survey.html) highlights how drastically holiday shopping patterns have changed in recent years.

According to the consulting firm’s annual holiday shopping survey, 22% of respondents plan to start their holiday shopping earlier than last year, and 28% of shoppers’ budgets are expected to be exhausted by the end of October — the highest level reported in six years. Beyond starting earlier, shoppers are also doing more of their shopping outside of Black Friday and Cyber Monday. Forty-two percent of respondents say they plan to participate in October sales events, an 18% increase over the past three years, and 1 in 4 shoppers say they even bought some holiday gifts during June promotional events.

Put together, it underscores that the holiday season is no longer a sprint — it’s a marathon. Even if consumers are starting their holiday shopping earlier, many of them are staying engaged all season long. It’s even more crucial than that from a supply chain perspective; retailers have enough inventory to last from October to December — and they don’t wait to put their best sellers on shelves for Black Friday.

“In general, shoppers are becoming much savvier and thoughtful about how they maximize their dollars,” Brian McCarthy, a principal in Deloitte’s strategy and analytics practice, said in a phone interview. Deloitte surveyed 4,000 consumers in the U.S. between Aug. 26 and Sept. 10. Consumers are doing more research, McCarthy said, and they know there are more promotional events they can take advantage of. In turn, “people are able to plan for \[these sales\] and lean into those moments with more intention.”

Deloitte has zeroed in on one type of shopper in particular that it calls the “holiday value seeker.” Thirty-eight percent of respondents fall into this category. Deloitte classified a respondent as a “holiday value seeker” if they agreed that they adopt at least five money-saving behaviors, like waiting for deals or switching brands when prices rise.

Being a value seeker “does not mean that these shoppers are not looking to spend,” McCarthy said. In fact, holiday value seekers planned to spend 12% more this holiday season compared to non-value seekers. They just do more research and are willing to make more trade-offs to get what they want and stretch their dollars further.

“They know how to use their loyalty programs and rewards, and they are willing to shift between national brand and private label to get more value,” McCarthy said.

Sixty-five percent of these value seekers are already holiday shopping during October, but interestingly, Deloitte said, their engagement is also more likely to hold through the full Thanksgiving promotional week. In other words, these shoppers are starting earlier, but they are more likely to stretch their spending across the full holiday season.

“I still think there is, to a degree, a finite amount of spend that will happen during the holiday season,” McCarthy said.

So, does that mean retailers now need to have their full holiday assortment on shelves starting the first week of October? Not necessarily, McCarthy said. There are certain big-ticket purchases — like televisions — that consumers may be more willing to pull the trigger on earlier if, say, they get a good deal in October. It’s also something they are likely only to buy one of during the holiday season, so retailers “probably want to win that one early.” But for other categories like apparel or toys, shoppers are more willing to make decisions later, outside of exclusive items, McCarthy said.

One thing that is certain about these value seekers is that they do a lot of research — they want the full picture on what kind of discount they are getting, how fast the shipping is, and whether or not they can use loyalty points before deciding whether or not to make a purchase, McCarthy said. In turn, not only do retailers need to make sure their product is in the right places, but they also have to make sure that the value proposition is “communicated in the right places,” McCarthy said.

“Retailers, in general, should try to make this concept of value easy to see,” he added.

## What we’ve covered

**Why Bogg is moving beyond its signature EVA beach bag** 

Bogg has earned a cult-like following in the past few years and surpassed $400 million in lifetime sales largely off the back of one product — a colorful and washable EVA tote. Customers like to take the bag to the beach, pool or park because it stands upright and is easy to clean. But the bag has an open top, which has alienated some potential new customers who wanted a more secure bag. Now, Bogg has an answer for those customers: The Go Tote, which Bogg founder Kim Vaccarella is calling its biggest product innovation in 15 years.

**Bath & Body Works is testing smaller-batch fragrances through Hype Lab** 

Bath & Body Works, like many sprawling brick-and-mortar retailers, is testing new ways to move faster on product development. The company recently built up an internal initiative called Hype Lab, which is all about releasing small-batch, limited-edition fragrances developed quickly based on social and cultural trends, as well as consumer feedback. Kristie Lewis, evp of merchandising at Bath & Body Works, who oversees Hype Lab, started creating her “ninja team” in May by pulling together different people from the digital, creative merchandising and in-house fragrance teams. The first fragrance out of Hype Lab — a trio of perfume mists inspired by viral desserts — was released in September.

Between travel and outings, festive apparel, and spiffing up seasonal décor, the holiday tab can add up fast—all before a single gift gets wrapped.

Average household spend is expected to increase to US$1,654, up 4% year over year, as 79% of respondents believe higher prices are in their future. As such, the value hunt is very much on. There’s plenty of room for delight, too. Half of the surveyed shoppers plan to gift an experience, up 11 percentage points since 2024, and most want to pair it with a physical gift. Self-gifting and luxury considerations are also rising, especially among younger generations.

Consumers are also getting an earlier start, with 22% saying they’ll shop sooner than last year. June promotions have already captured some holiday purchases for 1 in 4 shoppers, and October sales are gaining momentum (up 18 percentage points since 2023). The holiday shopping journey favors online-only retailers and mass merchants, which are expected to capture most of shoppers’ planned spend, while online spending is expected to make up 55% of retail budgets. Generative AI is a holiday-shopper helper, with 39% of respondents noting that it’s their primary tool for at least one holiday shopping task, but only 16% say they would permit it to complete a purchase.

Read on for key takeaways and [download](/content/dam/insights/articles/2026/amer189387_cic_holiday-retail-survey/pdf/DI_2026-Holiday-Retail-Survey.pdf) the full survey findings.

**Budgets get a jolly lift**

This holiday season, more shoppers (50%) plan to gift experiences, up 11 percentage points from 2024, with restaurant gift cards or in-person meals topping the list at 37%. Holiday value seekers (38% of surveyed shoppers), who engage in five or more cost-saving behaviors while holiday shopping, are likely to spend 12% more than other shoppers on average. They are also expected to begin shopping earlier and stay engaged through Thanksgiving week.

I sense a strong belief in the industry that a lot of AI traffic hides as, or arrives as, Direct in our analytics tools. I get where this comes from because I wrote about it:

- In our [AI Mode user behavior study](https://www.growth-memo.com/p/what-our-ai-mode-user-behavior-study), 18% of exits involved users leaving AI Mode and going directly to another site.
- In [Is AI cutting into your SEO conversions?](https://www.growth-memo.com/p/is-ai-cutting-into-your-seo-conversions), I described a potential journey from AI answers to brand recall to a direct visit, bypassing clicks.

Most of those visits came through Search (55.9% vs. 40.4% for other visits), and fewer through Direct (19.9% vs. 38.8%).

If you need to explain how AI is changing search behavior to your team, the [Premium Resource Library](https://www.growth-memo.com/p/exclusive-growth-premium-resources) includes an AI Mode User Behavior Deck.

There’s a plausible mechanism here, but is the signal strong enough to trace Direct traffic from AI in our analytics? Somewhat. And now, we have an example.

In an [interview](https://www.siegemedia.com/conversation/how-ramp-accurately-tracks-ai-traffic-w-eric-wiu) on the Siege Media Podcast, Growth expert [Eric Wu](https://www.linkedin.com/in/ericywu/) discussed how Ramp identified 30–40% of its direct traffic as originating from answer engines. I caught up with him and learned his team examined growth in Direct visits to long blog URLs that users were unlikely to type, filtered out patterns resembling email campaigns, and compared the remaining visits with organic search traffic. Some of that Direct traffic closely matched search visitors in time on page, scroll depth, and click behavior. Self-reported attribution confirmed that the users indeed came from AI.

That got me curious about whether the time is ripe to detect signal in our analytics. So, I went hunting for proof of hidden AI traffic.

## **Bots. Why did it have to be bots?**

I analyzed the Google Analytics 4 properties of 12 sites, using the same August–September 2026 comparison and excluding homepages, localized homepage roots, and unknown landings. Keep in mind that this small sample of 12 sites skews toward B2B, even though traffic is almost evenly split between B2B and B2C. All sites except 2 target the US.

At first, I got really excited: 8 out of 12 properties showed direct traffic growth from August to September! Some even over 100%. But when I dug deeper, much of that direct traffic turned out to be automated bot traffic. At one website, GA4 recorded 409,000 Direct sessions, of which only 198 counted as engaged.

Comparing the increase in all Direct sessions with engaged sessions alone shows a clear picture: engaged Direct traffic has been flat since the beginning of the year. **Across the filtered January–September sample, total Direct rose 140.9%, while engaged Direct changed −1.0% in monthly counts, or +2.3% in average daily volume** (when normalizing for days per month).

Conclusion: **I could not yet detect “hidden” AI traffic** without self-reported attribution like Eric and his team at Ramp. I also found that, on average across the 12 sites, Direct sessions with identifiable AI traces are only 0.003% of total direct traffic.

To uncover bot traffic, break Direct traffic down by day, landing page, country, browser, operating system, browser version, and screen size, and look for sudden growth concentrated in groups of visits with the same browser configuration and low or no engagement.

To find AI traffic, I excluded pages that typically get a high degree of direct visits, like pricing or login pages:

- Main homepages, regional root domains, index aliases, and untracked landing URLs.
- Subscription plans and pricing pages, including localized variations and donor-fee breakdown pages.
- Authentication portals, user registration, account management, dashboards, webmail, and internal app paths.
- Product demo requests, help docs, corporate about/team pages, investor relations, privacy policies, and internal search results.
- Transactional flows, payment processing, purchase confirmations, billing receipts, and automated system alerts.

I didn’t want to give up here. So, I ran a separate analysis of four brands to test whether greater AI visibility was followed by more branded search or Direct traffic. Across 632 tests, I compared weekly AI visibility with both measures at delays ranging from the same week to six weeks later.

The first results looked promising! One site showed a correlation of 0.72 between AI Share of Voice and Direct traffic, peaking at a three-week delay. Its correlation with branded search impressions reached 0.59. A second site showed a 0.47 correlation between ChatGPT mention rate and Direct traffic. Let’s go!

For the first site, the correlation peaked three weeks later, which made a delayed response look plausible.

Buuuuut a strong correlation needs a meaningful comparison. Two lines can move together because they share a trend, even without one driving the other. Correlation isn’t Cau… You know.

To check, I shifted the AI series against the traffic series, deliberately pairing different weeks while preserving the sequence within each series. I had tested seven delays and kept the strongest correlation, but tested each mismatched version only at that winning delay. So I repeated the test. **Amazon Ads VP Kelly MacLean on how AI helps marketers connect the dots across the customer journey, with lower costs and better delivery in early tests.**

Programmatic was supposed to make buying ads easier. For plenty of marketers, though, it made things more complicated. Amazon Ads thinks AI can finally close that gap.

On this episode of “Inside the Stack,” AdExchanger Editor-in-Chief Allison Schiff speaks with **Kelly MacLean, VP of science, engineering and product at Amazon Ads**, about the announcements that came out of Amazon unBoxed in September.

MacLean unpacks [Amazon’s new AI-powered ad platform](https://www.adexchanger.com/platforms/amazon-ads-and-the-amazon-dsp-get-an-agentic-rebrand/), which combines its ad console and DSP so advertisers can launch a programmatic campaign in as few as four clicks. She also explains what the marketer’s job looks like when AI handles the mechanics.

“The advertiser is owning the why and the what,” she says, “and then AI can help drive the how.”

Amazon Ads wants advertisers of every size to be able to use its DSP, not just those who already know programmatic. MacLean calls it “programmatic for everyone.”

That is a nice sentiment, but the proof is in the performance.

In beta tests, advertisers using Amazon Ads Agent to scale AI-driven campaigns saw 18% lower CPMs, 16% lower CPAs and a 65% improvement in delivery. “Those aren’t theoretical projections,” MacLean says. “Those are real live campaigns, budgets and measurable outcomes.”

MacLean gives credit to Amazon’s authenticated graph, which connects 90% of US households and allows AI to optimize against real purchase signals instead of proxies.

Access to real purchase data matters, MacLean says, because the consumer journey is never linear. A streaming TV impression might spark consideration, a display ad might reinforce it and an audio spot might close the sale. But a human managing four or five separate campaigns can’t necessarily make those connections.

Amazon’s edge comes from being able to see the whole journey, she says. “We want to make it easier for marketers to connect the dots wherever that’s happening,” MacLean says.

**Also in this episode**: How advertisers can move from simple campaigns to advanced settings as their trust in AI grows, why creative becomes a differentiator when execution is automated and why measurement is what MacLean calls the “validation layer” for AI-driven advertising.

# Love Actually’ reunions, delivered by DoorDash: Inside Anthropologie’s holiday sales pitch

*This story was originally published by Modern Retail’s sister site, [Glossy](https://www.glossy.co/).*

Anthropologie’s holiday campaign has a distinctly “Love Actually” feeling. The airport scenes in its “On My Way” mini film tap into that familiar arrivals-hall mood: the anticipation of seeing someone you’ve missed for a long time, and the happiness in finally being together. For the retailer, there is also a commercial opportunity in everything customers may buy along the way.

Launching October 19, the campaign spotlights products ranging from travel outfits and partywear to guest-bedroom updates, pajamas, and last-minute hostess gifts. Anthropologie is pairing that broader holiday wardrobe with an expanded food assortment, more home collaborations and a new DoorDash partnership, aiming to capture spending across the season’s smaller occasions.

“We know that we have a customer who loves to not only self-purchase but also look for gift-giving ideas,” said Anu Narayanan, global president of women’s, home and retail at Anthropologie. This year, she said, the focus extends to the preparations and personal moments surrounding those celebrations.

There is spending to compete for. The National Retail Federation forecasts that U.S. retail sales in November and December will rise 4.2% year over year to $1.013 trillion, excluding automobile dealers, gasoline stations and restaurants. Adobe expects online spending over the same period to rise 6.7% to $275.1 billion. But growth comes with price competition: Adobe forecasts apparel discounts will peak at 23% off list prices.

Alongside its airport-set mini film, Anthropologie has organized the campaign imagery around four holiday scenarios, each showcasing a different part of its assortment. Alongside the airport imagery, “Come On In” centers on Christmas at home; “Meet Me There” covers partywear; “Stay A While” features intimates and pajamas; and “Wish You Were Here” addresses resort dressing for warm-weather holiday trips. The range gives customers reasons to shop beyond a dress for one big night out.

The campaign will run across Anthropologie’s owned and paid channels, including Instagram, TikTok, YouTube and Facebook, as well as its own Substack. The brand has not specified which creative assets will appear on each platform.

“The holidays are all about finding our way back to the people we love,” Chief Creative Officer Jisoo Kang said in a statement. “Whether it’s a long flight home, a late-night drive or a quick ride across town, there’s something special about the anticipation of seeing someone again.”

In clothing, that translates into a less formal approach to festive dressing. Narayanan pointed to silky camisoles worn with cargo pants and sequined ballet flats, alongside the expected party dresses. Pull-on pants like the Maeve Marni (Donni- and Reformation-style taffeta trousers) with elastic or drawstring waistbands offer another option, while Fair Isle sweaters, soft joggers and a blue sherpa coat carry the travel story.

The holiday home assortment follows a similar logic: new sheets for overnight guests, mugs for morning coffee and faux-fur throws for the sofa. Anthropologie is expanding its food offerings with coffee syrups and cake mixes that can accompany gifts of mugs or bakeware. A “take and bake” approach encourages customers to bake something in a dish they can bring to a gathering.

That gives the retailer a way to sell several complementary items around one purchase. A PayPal survey of 2,005 U.S. adults, conducted by Morning Consult and released through PR Newswire in September, found that 58% felt greater financial concern heading into the holidays, yet 64% expected to spend the same or more than last year. Thirty-four percent said they would spend less on each individual gift to accommodate holiday spending.

Asked about value, Narayanan pointed to Anthropologie’s complimentary home and wardrobe styling services, which provide recommendations at different price points, and virtual appointments where customers can get help choosing gifts within a budget. The retailer will promote that support through holiday styling parties and store events in November and December. It has also reworked its online gift guide to make its recommended gifts easier to find.

“Sometimes styling seems intimidating,” she said. “You think that you either have to have a really big budget to work with a stylist, or you have to spend all this time. We want to prove that is not the case.”

DoorDash is intended to address more immediate needs. Narayanan described a forgotten hostess gift before a neighbor’s cookie exchange or shoes left behind while visiting family. The DoorDash partnership is available nationally in the U.S., with products automatically drawn from each store’s available inventory across apparel, home, gifting, beauty and accessories. According to information supplied by the brand’s DoorDash representative, delivery is free for DashPass members on Anthropologie orders of $20 or more, with a $1.99 delivery fee below that threshold. For nonmembers, the delivery fee is typically $3.99, though it varies by location and other factors.

Exclusivity is another part of the pitch to consumers. Anthropologie is bringing back its New York City Ballet partnership and collaborating on products with Suleika Jaouad and Jon Batiste, Susan Alexandra, and Molly Hatch, as well as nonalcoholic drinks brand Ghia.
