**Pixel Me Rollin’** 

After recent layoffs, Netflix headed into earnings with a fresh pitch to advertisers.

On Tuesday, Netflix unveiled what it calls the Netflix Pixel, an add-on to the conversion API (CAPI) it launched in March within the Netflix Ads Suite. The Pixel helps standardize the way marketers measure lower-funnel business outcomes, such as conversions. It also creates a way for brands to use this conversion data for audience segmentation and targeting, according to a [blog pos](https://about.netflix.com/en/news/netflix-ads-suite-has-better-buying-better-planning-better-results)t the company published Tuesday.

Netflix is also adding The Trade Desk to its list of DSPs that will have programmatic targeting available for Netflix ad inventory, starting next month. The streamer launched new targeting capabilities within Amazon DSP and Yahoo DSP earlier this year.

The new announcements came the same morning that Netflix reported its [third-quarter results](https://www.adexchanger.com/tv/netflix-touts-new-measurement-capabilities-as-it-struggles-with-modest-engagement-growth/).

Netflix touted 12% year-over-year revenue growth last quarter, which was in line with its forecast, but execs acknowledged during its earnings call that ad revenue growth in particular didn’t meet expectations. In January, Netflix shared its hope of [doubling its ad revenue again](https://www.adexchanger.com/streaming/netflix-doubled-its-ad-revenue-last-year-and-expects-to-do-the-same-in-2026/) this year.

The streamer hopes that beefing up its ad stack, including more programmatic demand sources and fancier targeting and measurement features, will work to woo more marketers into Netflix’s orbit.

**We’ll FTC About That**

The [acquisition](https://www.adexchanger.com/marketers/publicis-acquires-liveramp-in-a-major-shakeup-for-indie-data-collaboration/) of data collaboration platform LiveRamp by Publicis is one step closer to reality.

The Federal Trade Commission [approved the proposed acquisition](https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2026/10/ftc-order-preserves-competition-digital-advertising-ecosystem-part-publiciss-acquisition-liveramp) on Tuesday – although it imposed some conditions aimed at [preserving LiveRamp’s neutrality](https://www.adexchanger.com/data-driven-thinking/when-data-providers-get-acquired-neutrality-has-to-be-proven-not-promised/), to which Publicis has agreed.

Per the FTC, Publicis must guarantee neutral access to LiveRamp’s products and services. And it must set up firewalls that prevent it from using LiveRamp to access the data of competitors or their clients.

The FTC will impose these requirements on Publicis for five years, starting from when the acquisition officially closes (a date that has yet to be established). An independent auditor will periodically review Publicis for compliance with the FTC’s provisions.

Publicis has also promised not to retaliate against LiveRamp customers who raise compliance concerns with the FTC. On top of that, LiveRamp customers can request an audit at any time to check whether Publicis is complying with data security and privacy protections.

It’s notable that the FTC approved this acquisition without extracting any political concessions. Last summer, when the FTC [approved Omnicom’s merger with IPG](https://www.adexchanger.com/the-big-story/why-the-ftc-tied-the-omnicom-ipg-merger-to-brand-safety/), it did so on the condition that the combined holdco not “deny advertising dollars to media publishers based on their political or ideological viewpoint.”

Amazing how quickly the government’s priorities can change.

**The Untipped Applecart**

[Apple sent shockwaves through the online advertising industry](https://www.adexchanger.com/platforms/apple-publishes-its-plan-to-wipe-out-web-tracking/) with a Monday evening blog post penned by three WebKit engineers, who delivered the company’s clearest – and most decisively negative – assessment of the category to date.

The dark comedy here is that what’s a crisis for online advertising is a selling point for Apple, which spent the summer touting Safari’s tracker-blocking features in an [ad campaign](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Spb-ka7xrR8).

Meanwhile, outside the ad industry, Apple’s WebKit plans have barely registered.

The bigger news out of Cupertino is that Apple is reportedly preparing to debut its first touchscreen laptop and a foldable phone, according to [The Information](https://www.theinformation.com/newsletters/the-briefing/apple-pigs-fly).

Those are the developments likely to draw attention in the coming days and weeks, rather than anything Apple’s WebKit engineers have to say.

**But Wait! There’s More!** 

IAB Tech Lab CEO Tony Katsur has a reminder: ID vendors aren’t the only ones who have something to lose from Apple’s WebKit domain blocking. Publishers do, too. \[[LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/apple-domain-blocking-cost-publishers-anthony-katsur-n5e8e/)\]

A California judge ordered Meta to reveal which executives authorized the use of torrented content libraries for training the company’s AI models. \[[Torrent Freak](https://torrentfreak.com/judge-orders-meta-to-name-employees-who-approved-torrenting-annas-archive-and-libgen/)\]

Do you hear them?

The bells? *The drums*?

Apple is coming. And we’re not talking about 30%.

“It’s not enough to block cross-site cookies to prevent cross-site tracking today because the tracking industry has not stopped trying to track users on the web.” Those are the words of Apple WebKit software engineers John Wilander, Charlie Wolfe and Matthew Finkel in a [blog post](https://webkit.org/blog/18438/blocking-identity-resolution-infrastructure/) published Monday evening.

The post, titled “Blocking Identity Resolution Infrastructure,” is Apple’s most direct expression to date of contempt for the entire third-party ad tech and mar tech ecosystems. It’s also the first time Apple has laid down such a blatant plan to rid Apple devices of third-party web tracking.

“We do this because users deserve to not be tracked, not across websites and not covertly through fingerprinting, unless they explicitly opt in to it,” writes the Apple trio.

## **The Apple bites**

Apple isn’t taking this extreme policy step lightly.

The WebKit team argues that Apple has been pushed to this point. Blocking all cross-device cookies on Safari in 2020 was “a huge step forward for privacy on the open web,” they write.

But could tech vendors leave well enough alone? Not from Apple’s point of view.

“The tracking industry has not sat idle since,” they write.

Apple’s engineers note that mar tech, ad tech and all sorts of third-party tech and data vendors have rallied under new banners, such as “post-cookie tracking” and “identity resolution.”

An iPhone owner, for example, might sign up for a newsletter or log into a subscription assuming their email could be used by that service for follow-ups or outreach. But when that person unsubscribes from the newsletter or logs out, they’re unlikely to realize their email has already been absorbed into a network of ID graphs, where it can help build third-party profiles and continue to be used for targeting and tracking.

The ad tech and mar tech industries (“the tracking industry” is Apple’s internal nomenclature, apparently) have [already begun a major migration](https://www.adexchanger.com/platforms/how-data-and-ad-tech-vendors-are-preparing-for-the-ios-27-fallout/) from third-party services to a more first-party-based vendor approach – which is a big change.

For instance, LiveRamp’s bread and butter historically has been to serve as the central identity spine or ID graph for many large businesses and media companies. The same goes for its Authenticated Traffic Solution, a network of publisher-provided data. Together, these data assets strengthen the utility of its core RampID.

Switching to a first-party structure means LiveRamp (or any such identity/mar tech/CDP- type vendor) must instead narrow its identity graph to only the first-party data of each individual client. Five or so years ago, [this idea was known](https://www.adexchanger.com/data-driven-thinking/meet-the-four-horsemen-of-mobiles-answer-to-the-cookiepocalypse/) as a “bunkered” version of a data clean room.

In short, each first party has its own ID graph and therefore no first-party graphs can communicate directly. That’s very different from the marketplace relying on a shared identity that’s constantly being refined and expanded.

But that shift doesn’t necessarily get vendors off Apple’s blocklist. The WebKit team is clear in its blog post that even this first-party-based revolution is wholly inadequate and explicitly part of what is being expunged, starting with iOS 27.

Ouch.

“Even if identity graphs are only scoped to data from a single company, i.e. a first party, the central identity resolver is a third party and it holds cross-site, cross-device and cross-party data about the user and can perform matching and targeting functions in the capacity of a clearinghouse,” write the WebKitters. “That is a tracking capability that each first party does not have on their own.”

For vendors that are not themselves first-party data owners – such as login providers or newsletter services – the iOS 27 block will be in effect.

## **PrepTech**

So, is there anything third-party ad tech and mar tech vendors can do to continue targeting ads on Apple devices?

(crickets)

Seriously, though, the answer is “not much.”

The new iOS policy blocks email addresses and other data to their servers. “The blocking is done on the domain level,” per Apple’s engineers, “meaning they can’t just change the structure of the network request to work around the protection.”

For many vendors, shifting to first-party tech services was already a daunting enough prospect. And in Apple’s view, that may not even shield them from the crackdown.

There are, of course, quicker, less credible and therefore less sustainable workarounds. For example, some of the early ad tech companies targeted by iOS  – The Trade Desk, LiveRamp, Experian’s Audigent, ID5 and Permutive – quickly spun up new domains that weren’t on WebKit’s block list. One source familiar with Permutive’s strategy [noted that this tactic](https://www.adexchanger.com/platforms/how-data-and-ad-tech-vendors-are-preparing-for-the-ios-27-fallout/) is a temporary Band-Aid, not a solution.

And for the real ad tech nerds, check out this [esoteric Prebid GitHub example](https://github.com/prebid/Prebid.js/pull/15712). A few weeks ago – right around when AdExchanger [first broke news](https://www.adexchanger.com/platforms/apples-latest-operating-system-blocks-the-trade-desk-from-serving-ads-on-safari/) of Apple iOS 27 blocking key ad tech vendors – The Trade Desk created a new domain (TTDCDN.org) to serve as a secondary or backstop domain if/when its core ad-serving domain (adsrvr.org) were to be blocked by Apple.

But this is a losing game of cat and mouse.

In the WebKit team’s telling, “the tracking industry,” their catchall for everyone operating in the world of identity tech, mar tech and ad tech three-letter acronyms, has spent the past five years “usher\[ing in\] what they call the post cookie era.”

What else could Apple do other than “put strong protection in place” to deal with those post-cookie era solutions?

At this point, some industry sufferers might retort that nobody in the ad tech or mar tech spheres “ushered in” a post-cookie era. Apple did that when it unexpectedly began blocking cookies by default years ago.

Everything that’s happened since has been vendors just trying to get by in Apple’s post-cookie era.

WebKit is unlikely to find their arguments persuasive.

# [Blocking Identity Resolution Infrastructure](https://webkit.org/blog/18438/blocking-identity-resolution-infrastructure/)

Apple and WebKit have shipped protections against web tracking for a long time. We put privacy protections in place for cookies in the very first version of Safari, we invented storage and cache partitioning and shipped it ten years before other major browsers, and we’re actively fighting device fingerprinting.

We do this because users deserve to not be tracked, not across websites and not covertly through fingerprinting, unless they explicitly opt in to it. See [WebKit’s Tracking Prevention Policy](https://webkit.org/tracking-prevention-policy/) for a comprehensive overview.

## Identity Resolution, or the Post-Cookie Era

We fully blocked cross-site cookies six years ago. That was a huge step forward for privacy on the web.

However, the tracking industry has not sat idle since.

A “post-cookie” tracking method emerged, called *identity resolution*. In this scheme, third parties (i.e., not the website owner) invisibly collect your email address when you log in or sign up for a newsletter. They send the email address to their servers, create an opaque tracking ID permanently linked to your email address, and send that tracking ID back to the webpage. The tracking ID is stored on the website and can from thereon be used for arbitrary purposes linked to your email address, such as building a profile of your browsing or targeting ads at you across websites. Logging out or unsubscribing from that newsletter does not remove the tracking ID or your email address stored with the third party.

Over time, these third parties collect even more data as you log in using your email address or fill in forms with personal data. They use this to create a data profile of you, known as an *identity graph*. Here’s an illustrative example of what such a graph may look like:

Email addresses almost always constitute Personally Identifiable Information, or PII. Another example is your phone number. Such information not only allows for cross-site tracking, but also cross-*device* tracking. For the majority of users, their email address serves as a globally unique ID that they keep for years, even decades. When users provide information for one purpose, it breaks their expectation to use it for another unstated purpose. For example, a user who logs in or signs up for a newsletter is not expecting to have their information sent to a third party for other, potentially long-term, intents.

First party personalization is not tracking, and is not what our technologies seek to prevent. But even if identity graphs are only scoped to data from a single company, i.e. a first party, the central identity resolver is a third party and it holds cross-site, cross-device, and cross-party data about the user and can perform matching and targeting functions in the capacity of a clearinghouse. That is a tracking capability that each first party does not have on their own.

## What We Are Doing To Protect Users Against Identity Resolution

Some companies serve as third-party infrastructure to facilitate identity resolution. They are present but invisible on many webpages where you enter your email address or use your email address for login purposes. They are not themselves login providers or newsletter services, they’re just there to track you.

In our iOS, iPadOS, macOS, and visionOS 27 releases, Safari and WebKit block network access to identity resolution infrastructure to prevent cross-site tracking. This stops them from sending your email address to their servers and all the downstream effects of that. The blocking is done on the domain level, meaning they can’t just change the structure of the network request to work around the protection.

## Hide My Email

As an iCloud+ subscriber, you are offered the service [Hide My Email](https://support.apple.com/guide/icloud/what-you-can-do-with-icloud-and-hide-my-email-mme38e1602db/1.0/icloud/1.0) which enables you to submit unique, randomized email addresses to every new website while still getting their messages in your inbox. Unique, random email addresses provide additional protection against email-based tracking.

## Our Commitment to Web Privacy

It’s not enough to block cross-site cookies to prevent cross-site tracking today because the tracking industry has not stopped trying to track users on the web. They have ushered into what they call the post cookie era and in our latest releases we have put strong protection in place. We will continue to prevent covert and cross-site tracking by default, while maintaining the ability for websites to provide first-party personalization to their users.

By [Ryan Law](https://ahrefs.com/blog/author/ryan-law/)

Director of Content Marketing at Ahrefs

Gone are the days of compounding search traffic, ordinal search rankings, forecasting based on predictable click-through and conversion rates.

Today, your content pages are grist for the AI mill, their contents scraped from the page, blended together with competing pages, and shown to the user—if you're lucky—in a context and format controlled entirely by a third party.

Forgotten is the handshake agreement that good content will be rewarded by website visitors. Instead, most people who interact with your content will do so through an intermediary like [Google's AI Overviews](https://ahrefs.com/blog/google-ai-overviews/) or a ChatGPT response.

But most pages are still created with the assumption that people will visit them directly. How does content change if we abandon that idea?

I see more companies asking and answering this question, creating pages of information with the assumption that few people will ever visit them.

Instead, they seem intended solely for [retrieval by AI search engines](https://ahrefs.com/blog/retrieval-augmented-generation/) and synthesis into AI-generated snippets and summaries. You've probably seen them too.

These pages seem optimized not for human consumption but for [machine consumption](https://ahrefs.com/aeo/aeo-content).

They are terse and direct. They are crammed full of specific references: products, concepts, brands. They use strong declarative statements and back them up with clear, citable evidence. They're structured in rigorous topic clusters. They're updated with extreme regularity.

They're written for the widest possible audience in ELI5 English and, most important of all, contain none of the fripperies of "old-fashioned" writing: personal experiences and anecdotes, uncertainty and humility, colorful language, even illustrative images. They are usually AI-generated.

It is content that has abandoned the illusion that people will visit it. It isn't *bad* for people, per se, but it certainly isn't *intended* for them.

This is "headless content marketing": pages designed solely as vessels of information for influencing AI answers.

A headless CMS decouples page content from page design, letting you create and manage the nuts and bolts of your website's content before passing it to another service to actually show to users; headless content marketing does the same, providing information for AI search engines to present in whatever format they see fit.

I see this content cropping up on big brands with huge, established blogs—the brands who have felt the sting of [AI Overviews](https://ahrefs.com/blog/ai-overviews-reduce-clicks-update/) the hardest, and are looking for the next scalable distribution strategy for their content empires.

I think we'll see more of it. We seem destined for a world where big brands will maintain a library of headless content that is automatically updated, reviewed for accuracy, and systematically enriched with new data and research (probably by somebody called a [content engineer](https://ahrefs.com/blog/how-i-do-content-engineering-with-claude-code/)).

This content looks familiar to anyone who's done SEO for a long time. This is what search-optimized content used to look like, before the era of [Helpful Content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) and [EEAT](https://ahrefs.com/blog/eeat-seo/) guidelines; when all the Google PR bluster is stripped away, and just the rote mechanics of information retrieval are left behind.

And despite Google waging a long war against content written for machines, headless content is a logical response to the incentives Google has now created.

By [destroying click-through rates](https://ahrefs.com/blog/ai-overviews-reduce-clicks-update/) and [ordinal rankings](https://ahrefs.com/blog/ai-overview-change/), Google, ChatGPT, and other AI search engines have sent the implicit signal that on-page experience doesn't matter; all that matters is the information conveyed by a page. Headless content is a predictable consequence.

But there is a difference. Headless content can be high-quality in many dimensions. It can be direct and helpful, conveying useful information with extreme efficiency. It can contain [new and novel information](https://ahrefs.com/blog/information-gain/), sourced from original research or proprietary datasets or interviews. It can be accurate and updated to ensure that accuracy at a previously impossible cadence.

It can perform well in search…

...and AI search.

It doesn't look good—but that's the point. No one is supposed to *look*.

The goal of headless content is not to bring people to your website. Instead, it exists to help your [brand get mentioned in AI answers](https://ahrefs.com/aeo/brand-mentions), to help your domain appear as a cited source, to help influence business-critical narratives within generated responses, and avoid ceding important topics to your competitors. It plays by different rules. And that's important, because AI summaries seem to be a permanent feature of search. The game has changed.

Maybe content created for machines is no longer such a bad thing. Maybe we are increasing the quality and outcomes associated with AI-generated responses. Maybe this is what high-performing content looks like, under the new paradigm Google has created.

I think we're seeing a growing bifurcation in content marketing.

We're moving away from the messy middle ground where search content was expected to appeal to both human readers and [machine retrieval](https://ahrefs.com/aeo/technical-aeo). More companies are embracing the reality that content [optimized for AI search](https://ahrefs.com/aeo/aeo-content) looks different from content optimized for human interaction.

There is no guarantee that this is a lasting strategy. Headless content marketing is useful because AI search engines rely—perhaps over-rely—on [retrieval-augmented generation](https://ahrefs.com/blog/retrieval-augmented-generation/), rationalizing their answers by pulling relevant web pages from a search index.

But who's to say that will remain the case? Google seems intent on stopping ChatGPT from scraping its SERPs, and it seems that AI search providers are already realizing how [gameable RAG really is](https://ahrefs.com/blog/best-lists-research/).

At the least, headless content is a *logical* response to the incentives Google and ChatGPT have created. The only strategy that is utterly wrong is to keep doing what we have always done, and fail to acknowledge that the fundamental unit economics of content marketing and search have changed.

Google already decapitated your search content. Headless content just stops pretending otherwise.

Ryan Law is the Director of Content Marketing at Ahrefs. Before joining the team, Ryan was CMO at content marketing agency Animalz.

# AI boosts discovery but reviews still seal the deal, new research shows

This holiday season, shoppers aren’t blindly trusting AI assistants to do their shopping on their behalf.

According to a new [Feedviser](https://feedvisor.com/resources/e-commerce-strategies/amazon-consumer-buying-behavior-report-2026/) survey, ChatGPT is where 16% of shoppers start looking for products. However, only 9% go there to actually buy something. And when an AI assistant recommends a product, only 5% of respondents say they buy it on the spot, with the rest checking other platforms like Google and Amazon first for better prices.

For experts, this customer behavior signals that AI recommendations are a starting point, not the final word. Shoppers still check reviews, compare prices, visit retailer and brand sites, and look at shipping and return policies, for example, before deciding. The challenge for brands is to ensure these touchpoints reflect an accurate image of their offerings and ultimately convert customers.

PartnerCentric’s latest survey-based [findings](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260812208207/en/Shoppers-Who-Trust-AI-Are-6x-More-Likely-to-Trust-Creators-New-PartnerCentric-Research-Finds) show that, following an AI suggestion, 33% of shoppers go to check existing reviews, 22.3% compare prices, and 18.8% search Amazon or another retailer. Only 14.8% visit the brand’s website, while 7.6% look for creator content about the product. When it comes to brands’ holiday marketing reach, 33% of shoppers say shipping and return policies often or always change what they buy.

“AI is a starting point, not a final verdict,” said Stephanie Harris, founder and CEO of PartnerCentric. “The shoppers who trust it most are still checking the work.”

In PartnerCentric’s data, 42.2% of shoppers in the top two AI-trust categories still want reviews before acting, while 31.2% go to actually check the reviews right away. “So the recommendation has to survive the next question the shopper asks,” Harris said. “And that question usually gets answered in the reviews, on the retailer page, or in the shipping and return terms.”

Kieran Powell, executive vp at Channel V Media, which released its [The State of AI Adoption in America](https://channelvmedia.com/blog/state-of-ai-adoption-2026/) report this month, agreed that today AI is winning the research step of the customer journey.

As such, Powell said retailers should think of AI answer engines as a replacement for the Google search bar and blue recommendation links. “That is how consumers are most comfortable with AI recommendations right now,” said Powell. “The rest of the shopper journey still exists.”

Powell pointed to a recent survey by Prosper Insights & Analytics showing that consumers are using AI to shortlist products, but not to make their purchase decisions.

For example, 12.1% would let an AI agent find and book a restaurant on their behalf, 11.0% to buy groceries, 10.0% to run the smart home and 9.8% to pay their bills. Meanwhile, only 7.3% would let it buy apparel. “If people won’t let AI buy a $40 shirt for them, they won’t let it tell them which shirt is good,” Powell said.

Brands are increasingly realizing that being mentioned by AI assistants isn’t enough to get those customers to click purchase.

Musely, which offers prescription beauty and health treatments through its online platform, is one brand noticing the need to meet increased AI search demand with accurate product information and real reviews to convert potential customers. Musely has seen traffic from AI assistants grow steadily since 2025, so it’s currently focused on its GEO strategy to boost brand visibility and provide accurate information.

Paris Roche, head of strategic partnerships at Musely, said AI is becoming an increasingly important part of how consumers research healthcare, especially when they’re trying to understand ingredients, compare treatment options, read customer reviews or determine whether a brand is credible.

“For Musely, trust is especially important,” she said. Given that the company offers prescription medications across beauty and health, Roche said, “It’s critical that prospective patients have access to information that is not only easy to find, but also accurate and responsible.”

AI tools are making it easier for people to educate themselves before making a decision, Roche said.

“For us, the goal isn’t simply to be mentioned by AI,” Roche said. “It’s to make sure that when someone asks about Musely’s ingredients or one of our prescription treatments, the information being surfaced is clear, useful and accurate.”

With the upcoming holiday shopping rush, Harris said brands will still have to earn the recommendation. That’s because the AI assistants are reading the same ecosystem shoppers use to verify a product’s info, including reviews, product pages, retailer listings, creator content, pricing, shipping and returns.

In turn, Harris said the brands that go into the peak season with consistent proof of strategy already in place will be easier for AI to recommend and easier for shoppers to actually buy. “When those signals conflict, AI does not smooth it over,” she said. “It surfaces the gap sooner.”

# Kohl’s leans into clearer pricing, gift bundles and Uber Eats for the holidays

Kohl’s [is emphasizing](https://investors.kohls.com/news/news-details/2026/Kohls-Brings-Holiday-Magic-to-Life-for-Customers-with-Top-Gifts-Incredible-Savings-and-New-Ways-to-Shop/default.aspx) deep discounts and delivery capabilities in its pitch to cash-strapped shoppers this holiday season.

The retailer is more clearly marking items in its stores and online as being “X percent off” to help value-oriented shoppers. It’s also establishing $5, $10, $15 and $20 pricing tiers across categories and offering online and in-store buy-now, pay-later capabilities through Klarna. In addition, Kohl’s is adding more bundled gift sets and leaning into convenience through partnerships with DoorDash, Instacart and Uber Eats.

Kohl’s consistently pushes affordability in its messaging, but the company is making a more concerted effort this holiday season as shoppers deal with inflation, higher energy costs and tariff-driven price increases. A [recent National Retail Federation survey](https://nrf.com/media-center/press-releases/affordability-shapes-winter-holiday-shopping-according-to-nrf-holiday-survey) found that more than half of holiday shoppers (56%) say the state of the economy will affect their holiday spending plans this year. And data indicates that Kohl’s shoppers are already looking for deals. [Placer.ai found](https://www.placer.ai/anchor/articles/target-and-kohls-stand-out-in-octobers-deal-rush) that visits to Kohl’s during its October sale ran 9.6% above the recent same-weekday average.

Kohl’s knows it has “a responsibility to cut through with value,” Arianne Parisi, Kohl’s chief customer officer, told members of the media on Oct. 21. In today’s macroeconomic environment, Kohl’s is “thinking about how pinched consumers are \[at\] this time,” she added. But the company hasn’t always communicated that message effectively, executives acknowledged, which is why holiday shoppers will see more signs pointing to concrete discounts online and in stores.

“The data that we’ve seen is that we haven’t always been as clear about our prices and as clear about value,” said Ryan Waymire, Kohl’s chief merchandising officer. Signs like “50% off” make it “easy to do that calculation in your head” and stick to a $20 budget, he said.

Bundles are proving crucial to this messaging, as well. This year, Kohl’s will offer more than 400 gift sets, including from brands like Laneige, through its partnership with Sephora. Forty of those gift sets are exclusive to Sephora at Kohl’s. There will also be Advent calendars across categories, including toys.

“Anywhere we can bundle to provide a lower price per unit for the customers is a great gift and also great for self-purchase,” Waymire said.

[Like its competitor Target](https://www.modernretail.co/marketing/targets-holiday-push-stresses-affordability-exclusives-and-an-ai-assistant/), Kohl’s is playing up both its owned brands and national brands this holiday season. Shoppers can buy items from Sonoma Goods for Life and LC Lauren Conrad, as well as Nike, Under Armour and Adidas. More than half of Kohl’s gifting department is net new this year, and customers can snag sought-after toy brands like [NeeDoh](https://www.modernretail.co/technology/needohs-are-fetching-a-premium-on-resale-sites/) and Lego. “We definitely see squishies as a big opportunity,” Waymire said.

Kohl’s wants to ensure shoppers can buy these items both online and in stores, so it’s updating its inventory capabilities to keep more items in stock. During the holidays, more than 50% of Kohl’s digital orders are “touched by a store,” including through fulfillment, Parisi said. Kohl’s has more than 60 million active customers, and 80% of Americans live within 15 miles of a Kohl’s store, she said.

Delivery is top of mind for Kohl’s this November and December, too. The company is now live with Instacart and DoorDash and will launch with Uber Eats next month. About 80% of these partners’ same-day customers are net new to Kohl’s, Parisi said. This year will also be the first holiday season that Kohl’s customers can use Klarna’s buy-now, pay-later capabilities in stores and online.

Across channels, Kohl’s is emphasizing its holiday offerings through a marketing campaign called “The North Kohl’s.” The content focuses on themes such as coziness, style and home, and features actress Ellie Kemper as “Kohl’s Mom.” Kohl’s is also encouraging shoppers to use its [AI-powered shopping assistant](https://corporate.kohls.com/news/meet-kohls-new-ai-shopping-assistant-for-styling-inspiration-and-support). Still, the company is finding that most product discovery stems from traditional search.

Kohl’s holiday efforts come as the company attempts a turnaround under CEO Michael Bender, who took up the role in 2025. Kohl’s, once a department store giant, [lost nearly 70% of its stock value](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/06/27/how-kohls-lost-its-way-and-is-trying-to-become-relevant-again.html) in a five-year period. To spur growth, it’s now investing more in categories like fragrance, [expanding its private labels](https://www.retaildive.com/news/kohls-recovery-private-label-Q2-declines/758731/) and [scaling its creator efforts](https://www.modernretail.co/marketing/kohls-is-stepping-up-its-creator-efforts-as-it-attempts-a-sales-reset/). In August, [Kohl’s posted](https://corporate.kohls.com/news/kohls-reports-second-quarter-fiscal-2026-financial-results) a quarterly net sales decline of 0.9% year over year, but it also raised its full-year 2026 financial outlook.

As the fourth quarter is when Kohl’s sees most of its sales, the company hopes its holiday efforts will attract both new and loyal customers. “We’re thinking about serving our core, as well as resonating with the broader market and competing in what is a very competitive moment,” Parisi said.

Safari tracked down the trackers.

In a blog post this week, it confirmed what industry insiders already knew: Apple broke identity resolution companies’ ability to track users on the Safari web browser.

The move is just the latest in the cat-and-mouse game between Apple and advertising companies. Cookies with short expiration dates in Safari became blocked altogether. Apple also fought back against [CNAME cloaking](https://webkit.org/blog/11338/cname-cloaking-and-bounce-tracking-defense/) and other ways to triangulate identity without cookies.

To talk through Apple’s decision from the perspective of an ad tech and cybersecurity researcher, we bring on Zach Edwards, the founder of [DecryptAds](https://decryptads.com/).

Apple has the upper hand.

“It’s a cat and mouse game,” Edwards says. “And the cat can see basically everything the mouse is doing, and is just slowly putting their pieces in place to block that mouse in whatever escape route they’ve planned.”

While there are technical workarounds that might work – for now – to avoid Apple’s identity resolution blocking, he doesn’t see anything as being unblockable by Apple. Ad tech needs to get serious about consent and safer identity schemes.

**AI slop, monetized**

Then, we turn to Decrypt Ads’ recent [report](https://decryptads.com/blog/posts/ai-recipe-slop-networks.html) on 2,100 AI slop sites that, predictably, [forged connections to programmatic ad supply](https://www.adexchanger.com/programmatic/ai-slop-sites-are-on-the-rise-is-ad-tech-ready-for-its-new-mfa-challenge/).

Brands might not have expected that they were buying ads next to perplexing, AI-generated recipes purported to be written by fake chefs or other doctored authors. While there is a healthy debate about the value of AI-generated content, Google Search, for one, has [come out against “deceptive authorship,”](https://www.searchenginejournal.com/google-fake-author-warning-site-owner-guidance/591806/) such as content that tricks readers into thinking they’re reading something by a person, not a robot.

When it comes to ads showing up in unexpected places, ad tech has seen this movie before. From made-for-advertising (MFA) sites to toolbars to ad fraud to all manner of content farms, there are plenty of websites built to profit off display ads without making an investment into quality content. But while the game is familiar, AI slop will present its own unique challenges, Edwards warns.

”MFA websites are growing much faster than people are slowing them down,” he says.

# How QVC is building a flywheel across TikTok and TV ahead of the holidays

QVC is gearing up for what will be its 40th holiday season with a multi-pronged approach across TV, [TikTok](https://www.modernretail.co/technology/social-scrolling-is-the-new-channel-surfing-behind-qvcs-tiktok-strategy/) and more.

This season, the live-shopping giant [will offer gifts](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/qvc-unwraps-holiday-magic-with-danielle-fishel-as-its-mrs-claus-302915654.html) from brands including Le Creuset, KitchenAid, Laura Mercier and Nespresso, alongside QVC-exclusive launches from Off/Duty by Coco Rocha and RM Studio by Rebecca Minkoff. QVC will also hold its “Nonstop Holiday Party” event from Nov. 6-8, which will feature early Black Friday sales and special guests Martha Stewart, John Legend and Teri Hatcher. QVC has also appointed “Boy Meets World” star Danielle Fishel as Mrs. Claus in a marketing campaign.

QVC is one of the [originators of live commerce in the U.S.](https://www.modernretail.co/technology/the-case-for-and-against-live-shopping-in-the-u-s/), having launched in 1986.  But the company has also had to adapt as the format takes off. In April 2025, QVC [started streaming 24/7](https://www.qvcgrp.com/newsroom/pressrelease/qvc-group-launches-first-u-s-24-7-live-social-shopping-experience-with-tiktok-shop/) on TikTok. In addition to running its own [livestreams](https://www.modernretail.co/technology/big-name-brands-like-crocs-and-pacsun-are-powering-tiktok-shops-livestream-bet-but-us-shoppers-still-favor-short-videos/) and offering goods via TikTok Shop, QVC also works with hundreds of thousands of creators. QVC and its sibling HSN [acquired](https://www.qvcgrp.com/newsroom/happenings/qvc-group-is-named-seller-of-the-year-at-tiktok-shop-awards/) nearly 1 million new U.S. customers on TikTok Shop in 2025. Today, sellers showcase products from jewelry to pajamas via TV, QVC.com, the QVC app, social media and streaming platforms.

QVC is looking to have a banner holiday season as it tries to get back to growth. For years, QVC Group, Inc. — the parent company of QVC and HSN — weathered challenges, including declining cable viewership, tariffs and increased competition. [QVC Group declared Chapter 11 bankruptcy in April](https://restructuring.ra.kroll.com/QVC/) but [emerged from the proceedings in August](https://6abc.com/post/west-chester-based-qvc-emerges-chapter-11-bankruptcy-names-interim-ceo/19674167/) and reduced its debt by more than $5 billion. [QVC Group’s total net revenue](https://investors.qvcgrp.com/investors/sec-filings/all-sec-filings/content/0001254699-26-000018/qvc-20260630.htm) for the three months ending June 30 totaled $1.765 billion, down from $1.984 billion a year prior.

Modern Retail sat down with Krystyna Taheri, QVC Group’s SVP of social commerce, to chat more about how the company is approaching live selling this fall and winter.

**How are you thinking about live shopping now, compared to years past?**

“QVC’s been doing this for 40 years, and I would say we’re very good at experimenting in formats and style on TV. We still do about 60,000 hours a year of live TV. And then, on TikTok, we do about 200 hours a week of just live. While we’ll share some of the same products, we have different hosts. There’ll be some crossover, but we have TikTok-specific hosts.

It’s a different style of live selling. It’s a lot faster. You’re talking 20-second, 30-second hooks and sells, versus a seven- to eight-minute segment, which is what we do on TV. So that’s been a big fundamental shift. And there’s the technical side. We have 10 live studios that are built for TikTok. We’re filming with \[a phone\], and so, \[while\] we have a full robotics team for our TV studios that do the cameras, we don’t for TikTok. The sets are different. The cuts are different.

But I would say the core principles run across: establishing that trust \[with the viewer\], having that relationship, product demonstration, storytelling. Those are characteristics that you could put on either platform and be successful with.”

**How do you make a TikTok-optimized studio?**

“We have multiple channels, so our QVC main \[channel\] is more of a simple set. You’re going to have your shelvings, your branding. The QVC Fashion set looks like you’re in a closet. You have QVC Beauty, and that’s very up close, and \[hosts\] basically just have a tray, because you want to see the product and you want to see them put it on. Then, you have QVC Home, which has a fireplace, and it’s very homey. And then, we have a set that’s very kitchen-focused. We sell a lot of kitchen gadgets. We sell food. We’re working up to being able to cook live. So, you can transport yourself into these different spaces within your home, just like you could on TV. They’re just smaller.”

**For TikTok hosts and TV hosts, are there certain best practices you recommend? How do you coach people through the different formats?**

“It’s hard, and I would say it’s always a learning \[mentality\], because the TikTok platform changes a lot. The algorithm tries to be consistent, and sometimes, it’s not. For our TikTok live hosts, some already had a following. Some were fairly new. They just had very strong personalities and good selling habits. We picked a mix. … QVC has been amazing at finding talent and creating their own following.

\[The hosts\] do go through training. We teach them how they’ll have a schedule where they’ll go live, they’ll do some short-form content, and every week, they’ll do a tape review. They’ll sit with a producer and rewatch a really great segment of their live and maybe a not-great segment, and then talk about it. Like, ‘Maybe we could have tried this differently.’ ‘Maybe we should have done this.’ ‘This really worked.’

TikTok’s platform, like TV, is very analytical. So, part of the training is understanding what \[hosts\] should be watching while they’re live. How do they think about the click-through rate? How do they think about the click-to-order rate? Obviously, the revenue is an output of those metrics. So we try to teach them not to focus just on the revenue that’s coming in, but instead focus on those engagement metrics, because that will lead to conversions.

And then, we’re very adamant about aggressively testing and learning. \[The hosts\] will come with ideas. # How Stable Are AI Citations? 10 Things We Learned Tracking 37,500 Citations

SEO & Marketing Educator at Ahrefs

My colleague Glen Allsopp recently showed that [AI answers keep a small, steady core of brands and sources while the rest turns over daily](https://detailed.com/ai-volatility/). I wanted to know what happens to the citations that drop out. So we followed about 37,500 of them across five AI tools, every day for 20 days.

Key takeaways:

- **Treat citation volatility as normal**. It seems to be a built-in trait of AI answers, and it may change significantly with model updates. So, aim to appear more often over time, not to hold every citation without interruption. Because of that, AI citations might not be a great AEO KPI—brand mentions make a better candidate since they are more stable.
- **Don't judge AI visibility from one check.** 50–83% of citations are gone the next day, but about 75% of those come back within 20 days. Count how many of the last seven days you were cited.
- **Judge a drop by what came before it.** A citation that held for 8+ days almost always returned (96–99%). A one-day citation never came back 34–41% of the time.
- **Keep doing the SEO basics for Google's AI tools.** Rankings, traffic and a title that answers the question go with longer-lasting citations. More DR or backlinks beyond the basics don't.
- **Separate questions about your brand from broader discovery questions**. Being cited for your own pricing isn’t the same as appearing for “best X.” Track factual brand questions, reviews, and recommendations separately so a strong result in one group doesn’t hide a weak result in another.
- **Don’t credit a page edit for a single comeback.** Citations often disappear and return. Look for sustained improvement in how often you’re cited, rather than treating the next appearance as proof that your changes worked.
- **When a drop persists**, check the page’s search performance and how well it answers the question. Pages that rank in Google, get search traffic, and match the question keep their citations longer.

The article follows that order: how citations behave, how to tell a real loss from a blip, and what contributes to citations that last.

## How we measured AI citation stability across five AI tools over 20 days

My colleague Xibeijia Guan asked five AI tools the same questions every day for 20 days. She took every website cited on day one and followed it. Was it still cited the next day, and the day after? If it disappeared, did it ever come back?

Xibeijia's data covers one month. To see whether her patterns hold beyond that, we ran the same measurements on questions we track every day in [Brand Radar](https://ahrefs.com/brand-radar): 25 about AI visibility tools and marketing conferences, and 69 about SEO and marketing tools. Where our results back up or contradict hers, you'll find it in a "How solid is this?" note.

## Part 1: How often AI citations disappear and how quickly they return

Let's start with the most basic question: if an AI tool cites your page today, will it still cite it tomorrow? And if the citation disappears, does it come back?

### 1. Half or more of AI citations disappear by the next day

Across all five tools, at least half of the citations disappeared by the next day: around 60% on Google AI Mode and ChatGPT, 50% on AI Overviews, and 80% on Gemini and Copilot.

Gemini and Copilot looked less consistent, partly because their next answer often cited nobody. Exclude those answers, and all five tools looked similar: 50–60% of citations disappeared by the next answer that included citations.

Changing fan-out searches explains only part of the citation churn. Before answering, AI tools often run several web searches, known as fan-out searches. ChatGPT repeated exactly the same searches as the previous day, only 26% of the time.

But even when the searches stayed the same, its cited websites changed 81% of the time, compared with 91% when the searches changed. This suggests much of the churn happens after the search, when the AI decides which pages to cite.

Glen saw the same gap at the page level: AI Overviews cited about half of the same pages again the next day, and ChatGPT about a quarter. In Report A and in Report B’s August windows, about half the citations on Google’s tools and ChatGPT were gone by day two, too.

**Takeaway:** Don’t judge AI visibility from one check. For each question you track, count how many days out of the last seven you were cited.

### 2. About 75% of lost AI citations returned during the 20-day study; about half returned within three days

A missing citation isn't necessarily gone for good. Across all five AI tools, roughly 75% of citations that disappeared at least once returned within the 20-day study.

About half returned within three days. On Google AI Overviews and ChatGPT, around 40% came back after just one day without being cited.

Of all websites cited on day one, only 20–27% disappeared and never returned during the study, depending on the tool.

The Brand Radar reports we checked against showed a similar pattern, although slightly fewer citations returned (around two in three). Our figures may underestimate the return rate, since citations disappearing near the end of the study had less time to come back. We also tracked only the first disappearance, so we couldn't measure how often returning citations disappeared again.

The next-day return rates tell the same story. Only 14–25% of one-day citations returned the following day, compared with 69–87% of citations that had already lasted at least eight days.

A quick shoutout to our friends at [dofollow.com](https://trydofollow.io/Growth-Memo), whose Visibility+ service helps B2B SaaS brands identify where they’re missing from AI answers and traditional search. If you’re curious how your visibility stacks up against competitors, [see where your brand is missing →](https://trydofollow.io/Growth-Memo)

Organic search traffic melts 2-4x faster than the US Dollar. Between August 2024 and August 2026, inflation ate away about 6% of what a dollar can buy. Over the same period, [organic traffic fell 13% in the US and 24% in France](https://www.growth-memo.com/p/organic-traffic-is-down-but-its-not).

But it’s not all due to AI. Google has been showing more and sneakier search ads, plus it’s pickier about which sites it shows. And not every industry is equally affected. For example, publishers have lost \~42% in both markets while the smallest quartile stayed flat. Blaming every lost click on AI is a go-to avoidance mechanism for separating advertising, algorithm changes, and differences between websites instead.

That’s the synopsis of [part 1](https://www.growth-memo.com/p/organic-traffic-is-down-but-its-not) in this series. For part 2, I’m answering the logical follow-up question: if organic search dries up, **what marketing channels are growing?**

## **Email grows almost faster than paid search**

Two channels stand out in the [Similarweb](https://www.similarweb.com/) sample: email and paid search. Comparing January–August 2026 with the same months in 2025, email visits grew 16.3% in the US and 17.0% in France. Paid search grew 20.8% and 20.3%, respectively. Email still added more visits in absolute terms: 3.94 billion in the US versus 3.70 billion from paid search. In France, email added 462 million visits versus 401 million from paid search.

Caption: Same-period matching and strict nonmissing checks preserve these directions. Similarweb’s Email channel captures visits from webmail services like Gmail and Outlook on the web. Data excludes googleadservices.com.

But there’s a wrinkle in the data. One domain has an outsized effect on the paid-search numbers: **googleadservices.com**. It’s part of Google’s advertising infrastructure. When someone clicks an ad, a Google ad-services URL can help route or measure that interaction on the way to the advertiser’s site.

Similarweb estimates visits to that domain, but it isn’t a conventional website trying to attract customers. I excluded it from the charts above because I want to understand how traffic to websites is changing.

That choice matters. When I include the domain, paid-search growth falls from 20.8% to 13.5% in the US and from 20.3% to 10.7% in France. Similarweb’s estimated paid-search visits to the domain fell sharply, but we don’t know whether the drop reflects a change in ad activity, routing, measurement or some combination.

To see whether the pattern holds across the same websites, I narrowed the sample to 1,896 domains present in both countries, excluding googleadservices.com. Paid search grows 21.0% in the US and 15.2% in France; email grows 20.5% and 17.6%. With the domain included, the shared sample contains 1,897 sites and paid-search growth is 2.1% in the US and -7.3% in France.

The aggregate numbers don’t tell every site’s story. Back in the larger country-specific samples, the median site grew email traffic by 14.7% in the US and 17.7% in France. But the median US site grew paid-search traffic even faster: 17.4%. Main takeaway: Email’s growth extends beyond a few giant sites.

Some of the email traffic could come from functional emails like order confirmations or notifications. (And, those are obviously traffic gains that don’t tell us which channel produced more customers or profit.) But overall, I see email as severely underrated and a prime audience-building channel.

I’ve been pushing brands to build audiences on owned land, aka email, because no other asset is that portable and unfiltered than someone’s email address. Not even phone numbers, since most people don’t like to be called by sales reps. Most companies don’t do a good job at nurturing and engaging potential buyers via email, but it’s the least volatile acquisition and retention channel there is.

This memo examines the data when organic slows. Deciding what to do with the budget is a different job. The [Annual SEO/AEO Planning Workbook](https://members.growth-memo.com/resources/seo-planning-workbook) walks your team through 8 decisions, from replacing the traffic target to pitching the plan as risk management, and ends with a 1-page plan. [Premium subscribers have it in the library.](https://www.growth-memo.com/p/exclusive-growth-premium-resources)

## **Why I’m bullish on direct**

**Direct traffic is by far the largest traffic channel**: 43.5% in the US and 39% in France when we give every site equal weight and look at the median.

2 downsides to Direct: It’s shrinking (-2.7% US, -3.1% France YoY between January and August) and it’s a kitchen sink, including everything from dark social to non-referral advertising and word of mouth. That makes it hard to optimize, though not impossible.

But Direct has held up better than organic search. From August 2024 to August 2026, combined Direct visits fell 3.4% in the US and 5.3% in France, while organic visits fell 13.2% and 23.4% across the same respective sites. (This comparison uses a fixed set of sites with complete estimates for both channels. Sites with any missing months were left out, so both lines compare the same sites over time.)

In [part 1](https://www.growth-memo.com/p/organic-traffic-is-down-but-its-not), I found a split by website size: The median small site’s organic traffic was roughly flat, while the median large site lost 17.6% in the US and 26.0% in France. Direct shows a similar divide. The median small site gained 14.4% in the US and 21.2% in France, while the median large site lost 13.0% and 7.1%. The Direct comparison uses a slightly smaller sample with complete estimates for both channels.

News and information sites show a different side of Direct. Between August 2024 and August 2026, their combined Direct visits fell 30.7% in the US and 4.0% in France. The median French news site fell 20.6%, so the pooled result masks a much larger decline for the typical site. Separately, sites provisionally classified as editorial publishers across topics lost 34.4% in the US and 18.7% in France in combined Direct visits.

That raises a question about publisher brands. Weaker demand for those brands could be one explanation, but Direct also includes visits with unrecognized sources. The data can’t tell us how much of the decline comes from brand strength, changing habits, attribution, or domain changes.

If you run responsive search ads, Google is now steering more impressions toward whichever ad in an ad group carries the higher ad strength rating. That ad has the better conversion rate only 45% of the time.

A new study by [Brad Geddes](https://www.linkedin.com/in/ewhisper/), co-founder of Adalysis, analyzed more than 5,900 Google Ads accounts to answer a question PPC managers have argued about since RSAs became the default ad format. Does higher ad strength lead to better performance?

His answer is yes for some ads and no for others. The difference comes down to one setting, which is pinning.

I’ve known Brad since May 2011, when he became the PPC Faculty Chair at Market Motive while I was the faculty chair of Video and Content Marketing. And as one of the co-authors of [Digital Marketing Fundamentals](https://www.wiley.com/en-sg/shop/general-introductory-business-management/digital-marketing-fundamentals-omcp's-official-guide-to-omca-certification-p-9781119894575), which Wiley published in 2023, I asked Brad to contribute the chapter on Digital Advertising. So, I can vouch for his Experience, Expertise, Authoritativeness, and Trustworthiness (E-E-A-T) in PPC and paid media.

When Brad previewed the findings in a [LinkedIn post](https://www.linkedin.com/feed/update/urn:li:activity:7520864073555656705/) last week, calling ad strength “one of Google Ads’ most misunderstood metrics,” I went back to read [his full study](https://adalysis.com/blog/google-ads-data-study-does-a-higher-ad-strength-improve-your-performance/), which follows up on the company’s 2022 ad strength study. That gives us a four-year view of how Google’s ad serving has drifted.

Here is what the data shows, where it collides with what Google says, and what I’d change in your accounts before holiday traffic peaks.

## What Google Says Ad Strength Does

Start with the official position, because Brad’s numbers only become interesting against it.

[Google’s Help Center](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/9921843?hl=en) describes ad strength as a guide for the ad creation stage. It says the rating “doesn’t directly influence your ad’s serving eligibility” and isn’t used to calculate Ad Rank, Quality Score, or auction wins.

Ginny Marvin, Google’s Ads Product Liaison, has been just as direct. In a March 2024 [post on X](https://x.com/adsliaison/status/1773770107447103869), she wrote that ad strength “isn’t used directly in the auction & shouldn’t limit your testing.”

I take Google at its word on the mechanics. But “not an auction input” and “doesn’t affect which of your ads gets shown” are two different claims, and Brad’s data speaks to the second one.

## What Happens When 2 Ads Go Head To Head

The most useful part of Brad’s study isolates ad groups with two active RSAs that carry different ad strength ratings. Both ads share the same keywords, bids, and budget, which strips out a lot of noise.

In those ad groups, the higher-rated ad received more impressions 63% of the time. An Excellent ad beat a Poor ad on impressions in 78% of ad groups. Ads two ratings apart, such as Excellent versus Average or Good versus Poor, won 66% of the time. Even the closest matchup, Good versus Average, went to the higher-rated ad 59% of the time.

Performance told a different story.

The higher-rated ad had the higher CTR in 52.5% of ad groups, barely better than a coin flip. It had the higher conversion rate in only 45%, which means the lower-rated ad converted better in 55% of ad groups. On conversions per 1,000 impressions, a metric Adalysis calls CPI, the lower-rated ad won 54.3% of the time.

Then there’s cost. The lower-rated ad had the lower CPA in 51.5% of ad groups, and across all ad groups the higher-rated ads ran an 11.8% higher CPA. In Brad’s example, a lower-rated ad with a $100 CPA would face a higher-rated rival at $111.80.

Brad’s warning for anyone running ad tests is Google “will serve the higher-rated ad more often, even if it has a worse conversion rate or CPI.”

*See also: [Why a Sky-High CTR Does Not Mean Your Ads Are Actually Working](https://www.searchenginejournal.com/ctr-is-sky-high-in-2026-that-doesnt-mean-your-ads-are-working/577744/)*

## 4 Years Of Drift

Because Adalysis ran a similar study in 2022, Brad can show which way Google’s serving has moved.

Google is leaning harder on the higher-rated ad when it picks which ad to show, and that pick lines up with clicks a little better than it did four years ago. It does not line up with conversions any better. Brad concludes that Google “has increased its reliance on ad strength to determine what ad to show in an auction over the years.”

That’s his reading of observational data, and Google would likely dispute the word “reliance.”

## Why The Lower-Rated Ad Often Wins

Before anyone decides ad strength is useless, look at who the lower-rated ads are.

Brad attributes most of their conversion edge to pinning. In most of the mixed-strength ad groups, one ad was pinned and the other wasn’t. Pinned ads tend to earn lower ratings, and they also tend to post higher conversion rates.

That makes sense to anyone who has pinned a headline on purpose. You pin a price, a required disclaimer, or a qualifier because you want to filter the click rather than chase it. Ad strength rewards variety and keyword coverage, and a pinned ad written to pre-qualify buyers works against both.

The unpinned results look very different. Among unpinned ads, CTR rose with every step up in ad strength, and so did CPI. Conversion rates rose slightly at each step except Poor to Average. For those ads, Brad’s conclusion is that chasing a higher rating generally pays off.

So, the honest summary isn’t that ad strength doesn’t matter. It’s that ad strength predicts performance well when you leave Google’s system alone and poorly when you’ve deliberately overridden it.

*See also: [Google Ads Bid Strategy Testing: What Changed In 2026](https://www.searchenginejournal.com/how-to-test-a-new-bid-strategy-in-google-ads/571237/)*

## How Many Headlines Excellent Actually Takes

Only a third of unpinned ads in the dataset reached Excellent, and Brad’s asset counts show why stuffing in headlines won’t get you there.

Without pinning, an ad can reach Good with as few as seven assets. For Excellent, Brad recommends at least 11 different headlines. Volume alone doesn’t do it, though. Only 44% of ads with 15 or more headlines reached Excellent, and in the most extreme case, an ad with 38 assets was still rated Poor.

Once you pin, the minimum asset count to reach Good jumps to 10. Pinning two positions now caps an ad at Good and often leaves it at Poor or Average, which is stricter than what Adalysis saw in 2022. If you pin all three headline positions, Brad suggests aiming for about 13 assets.

There is a workaround. Pinning three or more different assets to the same position still leaves room for Excellent, while pinning only one or two caps the ad at Good. Position matters too

# Google Ads data study: Does a higher ad strength improve your performance?

By [Brad](https://adalysis.com/author/brad/) | 0 comments October 27, 2026

Categories

In 2022, we carried out a massive data study looking at ad strength. The results pointed in two directions:

- Ads with higher ad strength got more impressions
- Ads with lower ad strength had higher conversion rates

In other words, high ad strength came with more visibility, but that extra visibility didn’t convert as well.

That was four years ago, and a lot has changed since then. We reran the study to find out whether those findings still hold. We also wanted to answer the questions we hear most from advertisers:

- Is it worth aiming for an Excellent rating?
- How does ad strength affect impressions and conversion rates?
- What does it take to reach Excellent?
- How does pinning affect ad strength?

What happens when ads in the same ad group have different ad strengths? Here are our findings and advice on applying the insights to your campaigns. Jump to the end for notes about the over 5,900 accounts included in the data.

## What is ad strength?

Ad strength is Google’s measure of your responsive search ad’s relevance, quantity, and content diversity. Ratings range from Excellent to Poor.

As you build an ad, Google shows recommendations for improving its ad strength.

This advice is straightforward, but one recommendation deserves more attention: *Make your headlines more unique*.

When your ad assets combine benefits, keywords, and calls to action, your ad strength will increase. Often, so will your CTR and conversion rates. We could easily argue this is the most important factor when creating great ads.

If you pin assets, Google counts fewer unique lines, so this ad strength factor decreases.

These terms are also used throughout the study:

# The results: How ad strength and pinning affect performance

Many advertisers never pin; others always do. And some want to see all the data before they make up their minds. We’re going to get to the heart of the results and see how pinning and ad strength affect CTR, conversion rates, and CPI (conversions per 1000 impressions).

## For unpinned ads, higher ad strength means better results

Getting an unpinned ad to Excellent ad strength takes work. We wanted to know if that effort pays off.

To find out, we looked at ads for non-branded search terms to see if increasing ad strength leads to better results.

The charts below show **unweighted data**. This ensures ads with millions of impressions don’t skew the results over ads with lower impression counts.

#### Unweighted data: Ad strength metric comparisons

CPI is conversions per impression, multiplied by 1000 to make it easier to read. Since CPI combines CTR and conversion rate, it’s one of the best metrics for how effective an ad is.

CTR increases with every step up in ad strength. Conversion rates also rise slightly, with the small exception of Poor to Average ads. Since CTR improves quite dramatically, CPI also increases at each ad strength level.

We ran the same analysis on weighted and unweighted data, and the results were very similar. CTR and CPI rise with ad strength, and conversion rates generally do too.

This leads us to conclude that if you don’t pin your ads, you should aim for Excellent ad strength.

## Pinned ads benefit from higher ad strength too

Pinning usually lowers ad strength, so we wanted to see how pinned ads perform. To have a benchmark, we compared them with unpinned ads rated Excellent, which make up 33% of all unpinned ads.

#### Unweighted metrics by pinned combination

Most assets pinned to headline 2 pre-qualify users, which is common in B2B and industries targeting a very specific audience. It’s no surprise that ads pinning only this position have lower CPIs and conversion rates, when compared to advertisers who only pin headline 1, or headline 1 and 2.

The results for ads that pin headline 3 alongside headline 1 or 2 are harder to explain. These ads have the highest CTRs but the lowest conversion rates, even though headline 3 doesn’t show that often.

The stats above include pinned ads at every ad strength rating. We wanted to see whether higher ad strength makes a difference. That’s why we ran the same analysis on pinned ads rated Good and compared them with unpinned ads rated Excellent.

#### Pinned performance — Good ad strength

With Good ad strength, CTRs barely change, but conversion rates rise as more headlines are pinned. Pinning headline 3 makes the smallest impact, since it rarely shows.

Interestingly, the highest conversion rates came from fully pinned ads rated Poor. These ads had a single headline pinned to each position.

#### Unweighted ad strength data when all headlines are pinned

Higher ad strength improved CPI for every pinning combination except ads that pin every headline. Our [pinning study](https://adalysis.com/blog/data-study-5900-accounts-rsa-pinning/) found that advertisers who pin every line tend to be the most active ad testers. So their strong results are more likely due to rigorous testing than to Poor ad strength.

## Higher ad strength ads get more impressions but convert less

To see whether ad strength affects ad serving and performance, we compared ads within the same ad group.

For this part of the study, we refined the data to ad groups with:

- Exactly two RSAs
- RSAs with different ad strengths
- We kept our original criteria: non-brand ads with conversions and a minimum number of impressions

Both ads in each ad group used the exact same targeting methods. We also used an unweighted analysis, so ad groups with millions of impressions don’t skew the data over ad groups with only a few thousand.

### Ads with higher ad strength received more impressions in 63% of ad groups

The higher ad strength ad had more impressions in 63% of ad groups. Overall, these ads had 63% more impressions than the lower ad strength ads.

The greater the difference in ad strength, the more often the higher-rated ad received more impressions.

#### Unweighted data comparing ad strength to impression increases

Google consistently favors ads with higher ad strength. The biggest gap was Excellent vs. Poor, where the Excellent ad got more impressions in 78%.

When ads were two ratings apart (Excellent vs. Average, Good vs. Poor), the higher-rated ad got more impressions 66% of the time. The smallest gap was Good vs. Average, at 59%.

For testing, this means the greater the difference in ad strength, the longer it takes to reach statistical significance, since the lower-rated ad gets fewer impressions. # Which Types of Mentions Correlate the Strongest With AI Visibility? (260M AI Prompts Analyzed)

"Mentions are the new links" has become one of the most repeated phrases in AI search.

But which *kind* of mention?

In our previous research, we analyzed different brand factors alongside AI visibility—including web mentions, anchors, search volume, number of referring domains and so on.

This time, we zeroed in on brand mention **types.**

We compared seven of them, from Reddit threads to TikTok videos, with how often the same brand appears in AI answers.

In total, we studied 10,000 brands and 260M (non-branded) AI prompts.

Sidenote

Jump to our [methodology](https://ahrefs.com/blog/mention-types-ai-visibility/#methodology) for more information.

Use the results as a starting point for deciding where to focus your PR and brand-building efforts.

As always, a huge thanks to our data scientist [Xibeijia Guan](https://www.linkedin.com/in/xibeijia-guan/) for pulling the data together.

Key takeaways

- **Reddit** is the strongest signal with a \~0.75 correlation on the Spearman scale.
- **Press coverage** (0.67) doesn’t beat general webpage mentions (0.70)
- **ChatGPT** is the least tied to off-site mentions, across 6 of 7 factors
- Brands with 10x more **Reddit mentions** get about 5.5x more AI mentions.
- AI mentions rise with web page mentions, but with **diminishing returns**—a brand with 10x more web page mentions has only about 3.7x more AI mentions.

## Reddit mentions track AI visibility at 0.75, more than any other factor

Every mention type we studied correlated strongly with AI brand mentions across ChatGPT, AI Mode and AI Overviews—but none more so than Reddit.

1. **Reddit mentions (in ranking threads):** 0.75
2. **Domain mentions:** 0.70
3. **Webpage mentions:** 0.70
4. **Total traffic of webpage mentions:** 0.70
5. **News article mentions:** 0.67
6. **YouTube mentions:** 0.64
7. **TikTok mentions:** 0.60

The scores run from 0.59 to 0.75, where 1 would mean the brands rank in exactly the same order on both measures (off-site mentions and AI mentions).

The gap between the strongest and weakest factor here is small, meaning none of the seven mention types should be written off.

But, with a correlation of \~0.75, Reddit mentions (within the threads that rank in Google) track AI visibility more closely than any other factor.

That's partly by design: Reddit licenses its content to both [Google](https://www.pcmag.com/news/reddit-is-licensing-content-to-an-unnamed-ai-company) and [OpenAI](https://www.marketbeat.com/articles/reddit-poised-for-growth-with-data-licensing-and-openai-deal/), giving them direct access to its posts and comments to train their models and surface in AI answers.

Across [Brand Radar](https://ahrefs.com/brand-radar), our database of \~500M AI prompts, Reddit is also currently the second most cited source across ChatGPT, AI Mode and AI Overviews—just behind Wikipedia.

## Press coverage (0.67) doesn’t beat general webpage mentions (0.70)

Surprisingly, brand mentions in the press don’t seem to count for more.

"News article mentions" correlated a little less strongly with AI visibility than mentions across the web at large (0.67 combined versus 0.70).

In other words, press coverage still shows a strong positive correlation, but it doesn’t appear to carry extra weight than mentions on general webpages.

If you're planning earned media, aim for a wide spread of mentions across many sites as well as big-name coverage.

### Traffic-weighted mentions score 0.70, the same as raw mentions

Getting mentioned on a high-traffic page doesn't appear to win a brand any more AI visibility than getting mentioned on a quiet one.

When we looked at combined correlations across all three AI platforms, "Webpage mentions" and "Total traffic of webpage mentions" both scored 0.70.

This means pitching small, niche sites may get you just as much AI visibility as pitching large publications, because a mention on a low-traffic page seems to count about as much.

Sidenote

You may be wondering why the combined values in this chart are higher than the individual values. When we studied a single AI platform, lots of brands were invisible (46% in ChatGPT, 23% in AI Mode and 18% in AI Overviews). But, across all three, only 14% truly received zero AI mentions, because a brand that one AI platform failed to mention was usually visible on another. Brands at zero are hard to tell apart, so when there’s fewer of them, the link between web mentions and AI mentions is easier to see.

### ChatGPT is the least dependent on off-site mentions, across 6 of 7 factors

ChatGPT tracks off-site mentions slightly less closely than AI Mode or AI Overviews, so mentions are a slightly weaker guide to visibility there.

You can see this in the heat map above, where ChatGPT’s correlations are mostly yellow (0.60 to 0.65)—meaning they're slightly weaker—while AI Mode and AI Overviews are mostly orange and green.

Still, the factors rank in roughly the same order on all three platforms.

## Brands with 10x more webpage mentions get 3.7x more AI mentions

Web mentions and AI mentions rise together, so we measured how many extra AI mentions a brand typically gets as its webpage coverage grows.

For example, if one brand is mentioned on 1,000 pages and another on 10,000, the second would typically show up in AI answers about 3.7 times as often.

This pattern applies to every platform, though it's strongest on AI Overviews (3.5x) and weakest on ChatGPT (2.2x).

### AI visibility grows slower than web mentions (3.7x vs 10x)

AI mentions don't grow one-for-one with coverage.

If a page receives 10x more webpage mentions, it only earns 3.7x more AI mentions.

In the table above, going from 1,000 to 10,000 webpage mentions takes 9,000 new pages, but only adds around 200 AI mentions.

These are correlations, so we can’t say for certain that more mentions *cause* more AI visibility.

But if they do, you shouldn’t expect a handful of new mentions to help your brand show up in AI answers.

If you want a visible change in AI visibility, you probably need a large, sustained increase in the number of sites talking about you, and you should track your progress over months rather than weeks.

Bear in mind, this multiplier isn't the same for every mention type.

A brand with 10x more Reddit mentions, for example, tends to get about 5.5x more AI mentions.

The typical (median) brand in our study had just 8 Reddit threads mentioning it, and 29% had none at all.

Check how many Reddit threads mention you in [Brand Radar](https://ahrefs.com/brand-radar).

If there are 8 or more, you are ahead of half the brands we studied.

## Brand size explains part of the link, but not all of it

When we last published this study, one of the most common questions we got was: are these correlations just showing us the shape of a big brand?

In other words, were the strong links between web mentions and AI mentions just the ef
